places.location_context: Allatkerti korut in the City Park, between the zoo and the Szechenyi thermal baths, a fifteen-minute metro ride from the centre.
places.time_needed: Two hours.
places.verdict: Go for the room and the pancake. Book dinner rather than lunch, and pair it with the baths across the park.

places.name: Hungarian National Museum
places.headline: Three and a Half Thousand Forint for the Building the Revolution Started On
places.body:
The Hungarian National Museum charges 3,500 HUF for a full-price adult ticket, with a discounted adult ticket for Hungarian and EEA citizens at 1,750 HUF. It opens Tuesday to Sunday from 10am to 6pm and is closed on Mondays.

This is the national collection, which in Hungary means the crown jewels of the story the country tells about itself: the coronation mantle, the Roman stones, the Ottoman centuries, the 1848 revolution, the twentieth century that kept happening to Hungary rather than being chosen by it.

It is also a building with a specific place in that story. Sandor Petofi is said to have recited the National Song from its steps on 15 March 1848, and whether or not he actually stood there, the country has decided he did. The steps are still where the national holiday happens.
places.what_great: One coherent national narrative rather than a warehouse of objects, in a serious neoclassical building that is itself part of the history. The permanent exhibitions are free on the third Saturday of every month for Hungarian and EEA citizens. Rarely crowded compared to the thermal baths and the parliament.
places.what_ruined: Labelling in English is thinner than in Hungarian, and some rooms assume you already know the outline of Hungarian history. The full-price ticket at 3,500 forint is double what an EEA citizen pays, which is legal and common in the region but still stings. Closed Mondays, which catches people.
places.rating_rationale: Four for a strong, coherent collection let down slightly by English labelling. Five for safety in a calm museum district. Four for value: 3,500 forint is fair, but the two-tier pricing means visitors pay twice what locals do.
places.meta_description: The Hungarian National Museum costs 3,500 HUF for adults, open Tuesday to Sunday, 10am to 6pm. The national collection, in the building 1848 used as a stage.

places.what_it_is: Hungary's national museum, founded in 1802, holding the country's historical collections from the Roman period through the twentieth century in a neoclassical building on Muzeum korut.
places.why_go: It is the single best place to get the shape of Hungarian history before you look at anything else in Budapest. The city makes far more sense afterwards, particularly the parts of it that were built to make a political point.
places.the_good: A clear chronological run through a complicated national story, strong holdings on 1848 and on the Ottoman period, and a building that is part of the history it houses. Free on the third Saturday of the month for Hungarian and EEA citizens.
places.the_downsides: English labelling thins out in places and assumes background knowledge. Non-EEA visitors pay double the local rate. It is closed on Mondays.
places.best_for: Anyone who wants the context before the sightseeing, and anyone interested in 1848 or in how central European countries narrate their own past.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Budapest and it is a baths-and-Danube day. This rewards an unhurried couple of hours, not a rushed thirty minutes.
places.practical: Go on a weekday morning. Read the 1848 rooms properly even if you skim elsewhere, because they explain the steps outside. Allow time for the building itself.
places.tickets: Full-price adult admission is 3,500 HUF. Hungarian and EEA citizens pay a discounted 1,750 HUF, and the permanent exhibitions are free to them on the third Saturday of each month. Group tickets for more than ten people are 3,000 HUF per person.
places.getting_there: Metro line 3 or 4 to Kalvin ter, then a two-minute walk up Muzeum korut. It sits between the Jewish quarter and the river, so it folds easily into a walking day.
places.location_context: Muzeum korut, on the edge of District VIII, with the university quarter on one side and Kalvin ter on the other. The garden in front is a genuine public space, busy with students in warm weather.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the permanent exhibitions at a reasonable pace.
places.accessibility: The main building has lifts serving the exhibition floors; the front steps are the ceremonial entrance rather than the accessible one.
places.verdict: Go first, not last. Three and a half thousand forint buys the context that makes the rest of Budapest legible, and the building is where the country's founding modern story is set.

places.name: MALBA
places.headline: Twelve Thousand Pesos, or Six Thousand If You Come on a Wednesday
places.body:
MALBA charges 12,000 pesos for general admission on Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and 6,000 pesos for students, teachers and pensioners with accreditation. On Wednesdays general admission is 6,000 pesos. Children under 5 enter free.

The collection is Latin American art of the twentieth century, and it is the best of its kind: Frida Kahlo's Self-portrait with Monkey and Parrot, Diego Rivera, Tarsila do Amaral's Abaporu, Antonio Berni, Xul Solar. Argentina has a habit of exporting its artists, and this is where the argument for keeping them is made.

The building in Palermo is a clean, light 2001 design that does not fight the work, and there is a cinema on the first floor running during normal museum hours.
places.what_great: The strongest twentieth-century Latin American collection anywhere, half price on Wednesdays, and a building that gets out of the way. The cinema programme is genuinely good and separately ticketed.
places.what_ruined: The permanent collection is not large and can be walked in an hour. Argentine prices move fast, so anything printed about the cost is out of date quickly. Palermo puts it a taxi or a long walk from the centre.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the collection, which has no equal in the region. Four for safety: Palermo is one of the safer parts of Buenos Aires but ordinary city caution applies. Five for value, particularly on a Wednesday.
places.meta_description: MALBA in Buenos Aires costs 12,000 pesos general admission and 6,000 on Wednesdays. The best collection of twentieth-century Latin American art anywhere.

places.what_it_is: The Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires, in Palermo, holding twentieth-century Latin American painting and sculpture alongside temporary exhibitions and a cinema.
places.why_go: Because Latin American modernism is treated here as a subject in its own right rather than a footnote to Europe, and because the Kahlo and the Abaporu are both in this building.
places.the_good: A tightly chosen collection with no filler, half-price Wednesdays, a good cinema, and a building designed for looking at paintings.
places.the_downsides: Small permanent collection. Prices change frequently with inflation. Not walkable from the centre. Closed Tuesdays.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in modern art, and anyone who wants to understand what Argentina thinks of itself.
places.skip_if: You have one day and it is a Recoleta cemetery and steak day. This wants unhurried attention.
places.practical: Come on a Wednesday for half price. Check the cinema listing before you go, because the programme is better than most cinemas in the city. Combine it with the Botanical Garden and Palermo's parks, which are minutes away.
places.tickets: General admission 12,000 pesos; students, teachers and pensioners with accreditation 6,000 pesos; under-5s free. On Wednesdays general admission is 6,000 pesos and concessions 3,000. Cinema tickets are priced separately at 8,000 pesos general.
places.getting_there: Bus 67, 102 or 130 to Avenida Figueroa Alcorta, or a fifteen-minute taxi from the centre. The nearest subte stations are a long walk away.
places.location_context: Palermo, on Figueroa Alcorta beside the parks, close to the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes and the botanical garden, in the greenest part of the city.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours.
places.accessibility: Step-free throughout with lifts to all floors, and free admission for people with disabilities.
places.verdict: Go on a Wednesday for half price. The best Latin American collection anywhere, in a building that knows to stay quiet.

places.name: Design Museum Denmark
places.headline: A Hundred and Forty Kroner for Why Your Chair Looks Like That
places.body:
Design Museum Denmark charges DKK 140 for adults, DKK 90 for under-27s and students with valid ID, and admits children under 18 free. It opens daily from 10.00 to 18.00, with late opening until 20.00 on Thursdays.

The museum is the answer to a question most visitors to Copenhagen arrive already asking: why does everything here look like that. The Danish Chair gallery alone lines up the twentieth century's most copied furniture in one long room, and seeing the originals in sequence makes the copies in every airport lounge on earth suddenly legible.

It is housed in an eighteenth-century former hospital in Frederiksstaden, a few minutes from Amalienborg, which gives the collection a set of calm rooms and a courtyard garden that most design museums would envy.
places.what_great: The Danish Chair gallery, which is the clearest single exhibit about modern design anywhere. Free for under-18s. The building and its garden are worth the visit on their own, and the late Thursday opening is genuinely useful.
places.what_ruined: A hundred and forty kroner is steep for a museum you can see in ninety minutes, and Copenhagen is expensive enough already. The collection is narrow by design, so if you are not interested in objects you will be finished quickly.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a museum that does one thing better than anyone else. Five for safety in Frederiksstaden. Four for value, because DKK 140 is a lot for ninety minutes even when those ninety minutes are excellent.

places.what_it_is: Denmark's national museum of design and applied arts, in a converted eighteenth-century hospital in Frederiksstaden, best known for its gallery of twentieth-century Danish chairs.
places.why_go: Because Danish design is the thing Copenhagen is most famous for, and this is where you can see the originals rather than the version of them sold at every furniture chain in the world.
places.the_good: The Danish Chair gallery. Free entry for under-18s. A calm building with a courtyard garden, late opening on Thursdays, and a shop that is actually good.
places.the_downsides: Expensive for its size. Deliberately narrow in scope. If you are not curious about objects and how they are made, ninety minutes will feel like plenty.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in furniture, industrial design or craft, and families, given free entry for under-18s.
places.skip_if: You are indifferent to design objects. There is no broad art collection here to fall back on.
places.practical: The ticket office closes an hour before the museum does. Thursday evening is the quietest slot. Combine it with Amalienborg and the harbour walk, which are both minutes away.
places.tickets: Adults pay DKK 140. Under-27s and students with valid ID and student card pay DKK 90. Children under 18 enter free. Groups of ten or more pay DKK 110 per person.
places.getting_there: A fifteen-minute walk from Kongens Nytorv metro, or a short walk north from Nyhavn past Amalienborg. Bus 1A stops nearby.
places.location_context: Bredgade in Frederiksstaden, the eighteenth-century royal quarter, a few minutes from Amalienborg Palace and the Marble Church, and within easy walking distance of Nyhavn.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours, longer if the temporary exhibition interests you.
places.accessibility: Step-free access with lifts to the exhibition floors and accessible toilets.
places.verdict: The best ninety minutes in Copenhagen if you care at all about how objects are made. Free for under-18s, late on Thursdays, and the chair gallery alone justifies the hundred and forty kroner.

places.name: Hotel d'Angleterre
places.headline: Ninety-Two Rooms on the Best Square in Copenhagen
places.body:
Hotel d'Angleterre has 92 rooms including 55 suites, and sits at Kongens Nytorv 34 in the historic centre. Rates are not published as a fixed figure and move with season and availability, so treat any number quoted elsewhere with suspicion.

It has been a hotel since 1755 and occupies the whole north side of Kongens Nytorv, which is the square Nyhavn runs off and where the metro, the royal theatre and Stroget all meet. If you want to walk everywhere in Copenhagen, this is the address that makes that true.

What you are paying for is position and the standard of a properly staffed grand hotel: a Michelin-starred restaurant on site, a spa in the basement, and a concierge who will actually be useful.
places.what_great: The best-placed hotel in Copenhagen, with Nyhavn, the metro and the shopping street all within two minutes. Ninety-two rooms, large enough to be properly staffed and small enough to be attentive.
places.what_ruined: Very expensive, and the published rates are promotional rather than a real price list, so budgeting means getting a quote. Kongens Nytorv is a working square with traffic and, in summer, a constant flow of people. Grand-hotel formality is not to everyone's taste.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the hotel and its position. Five for safety on Kongens Nytorv. Three for value: a top-of-market price in an expensive city, defensible for the location and not otherwise.

places.name: Noma
places.headline: Four and a Half Thousand Kroner Before You Order a Drink
places.body:
Noma charges 4,500 DKK for the menu, with a wine pairing at 2,000 DKK and a juice pairing at 1,500 DKK. It serves Wednesday to Saturday from 17:00 to 23:00 and is closed Sunday, Monday and Tuesday.

That is roughly 600 euros a head with wine, which makes this one of the most expensive meals in Europe and the single largest line on most people's Copenhagen budget. What it buys is the restaurant that rewrote what Nordic food is, across three seasonal menus a year: ocean, vegetable and forest.

Reservations open to a newsletter list rather than a booking page, in seasonal releases that go in minutes. If you are reading this hoping to eat next week, you will not be eating next week.
places.what_great: The most influential restaurant of the last twenty years, still cooking at that level. Three genuinely different menus across the year. Service that is warm rather than reverent, which at this price is rarer than the food.
places.what_ruined: Four and a half thousand kroner before drinks, and the pairings add another two thousand. Booking is a newsletter lottery, not a reservation system. Closed three days a week. Refshaleoen is a taxi or a long cycle from the centre.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the cooking, which is as good as it is claimed to be. Five for safety. Two for value: it is defensible as a once-in-a-lifetime meal and indefensible as an ordinary one, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest at 4,500 kroner.

places.name: Museum of the Future
places.headline: A Hundred and Sixty-Nine Dirhams for a Building Pretending to Be a Museum
places.body:
The Museum of the Future charges 169 AED for an entry ticket for visitors aged four and over. It opens every day from 10:00 am to 7:00 pm, with last admission at 5:00 pm.

The building is the attraction: a silver torus covered in Arabic calligraphy, with a void through the middle and no visible columns. It is one of the genuinely striking pieces of architecture built anywhere this century, and Dubai knows it.

Inside is not a museum in any conventional sense. It is a sequence of immersive, theatrical sets about space stations, bioengineering and wellness, closer to a very expensive themed experience than to a collection. Whether that is worth 169 dirhams depends entirely on what you thought you were buying.
places.what_great: The building, inside and out, is extraordinary and photographs badly compared to standing in it. The set design and production values are as high as anything in the world. Timed entry keeps it from becoming a crush.
places.what_ruined: There is no collection, nothing old and nothing that will surprise a sceptic. A hundred and sixty-nine dirhams is a lot for roughly ninety minutes. It sells out days ahead, and the ticket is date and time specific with no flexibility.
places.rating_rationale: Four for an experience nowhere else does at this level. Five for safety in Dubai. Three for value: 169 dirhams for ninety minutes of theatre without a single object is a lot, however good the theatre is.
places.meta_description: The Museum of the Future in Dubai costs 169 AED, open daily 10am to 7pm with last admission at 5pm. An extraordinary building around an experience, not a collection.

places.verdict: Go for the building, not the content, and book days ahead. If you want objects and history, spend the 169 dirhams elsewhere.

places.name: Book of Kells Experience at Trinity College
places.headline: Twenty-Six Euros for a Ninth-Century Manuscript and the Room It Lives In
places.body:
The Book of Kells Experience at Trinity College starts at 26 euros per person, and the standard visit runs about 90 minutes.

It is worth being precise about what you see, because this is where expectations go wrong. The Book of Kells is displayed as two open pages under glass, and you file past them. The manuscript is astonishing and the display is necessarily brief. What most visitors remember instead is the Long Room, the barrel-vaulted eighteenth-century library upstairs, which is one of the most photographed interiors in Europe and deserves it.

Trinity students and staff visit free of charge and can bring up to two guests, which is worth knowing if you have any connection to the college.
places.what_great: The Long Room is spectacular and justifies the ticket largely on its own. The digital exhibition around the manuscript does a real job of explaining what you are looking at. Trinity students, staff and alumni go free and can bring up to two guests.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-six euros is steep for what is, at the manuscript itself, a filed-past view of two pages. The route is one-way and paced by the group. The college is in the middle of Dublin and the surrounding streets are among the busiest in the city, so arriving is rarely calm.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the Long Room is genuinely one of the great library interiors and the manuscript is extraordinary. Value is three: 26 euros is a lot when the manuscript itself is two open pages behind glass.
places.meta_description: The Book of Kells Experience starts at 26 euros per person. What you actually see, why the Long Room matters more, and how to time it.

places.practical: Book a timed slot in advance, since this is among the busiest paid attractions in Ireland. Early slots are calmer. Give the Long Room more of your time than the manuscript, which is the reverse of what most people plan.

places.name: Chapter One
places.headline: Ninety-Five Euros for Lunch, a Hundred and Fifty for the Surprise
places.body:
Chapter One charges 95 euros for a three-course lunch and 150 euros for the surprise tasting menu, with an additional selection of artisan cheeses at 29 euros.

It sits in the basement of the Dublin Writers Museum on Parnell Square, which gives it low ceilings, thick walls and none of the glass-box quality that afflicts restaurants at this level. The cooking is French technique applied to Irish produce, and it has held Michelin recognition for over two decades.

The lunch menu is the value proposition here. Ninety-five euros is a great deal of money and is also roughly two thirds of what the same kitchen costs in the evening.
places.what_great: Cooking at the top of the Irish market. A basement dining room with genuine atmosphere rather than designed neutrality. Lunch at 95 euros, which is the cheapest way into this kitchen.
places.what_ruined: It is very expensive whichever menu you take. The cheese supplement at 29 euros on top of a 95 euro lunch is steep. Parnell Square north is a quieter and scruffier part of the city than the price suggests.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the cooking and the room together. Four for safety: Parnell Square is fine but the north inner city warrants ordinary caution at night. Three for value, because 95 euros for lunch is a genuine expense however good it is.

places.name: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
places.headline: Twenty-Two Online, Twenty-Four at the Door, and No Objects At All
places.body:
EPIC charges 22.00 euros for an adult aged 18 to 64 booking online and 24.00 on the day, with teenagers aged 13 to 17 at 15.00 online and 16.00 on the day.

The thing to understand before buying is that EPIC has no collection. It is a fully digital museum in the vaults of the CHQ building, telling the story of Irish emigration through twenty rooms of screens, projections and interactive galleries. There are no objects.

That is either the appeal or the problem, and which one it is for you is worth deciding in advance. It handles a diffuse, unphotogenic subject, thirty million people leaving over three centuries, better than an artefact museum could. But visitors expecting a traditional museum sometimes feel they have paid 22 euros for a very good exhibition rather than a collection.
places.what_great: It solves a genuinely hard problem: how to tell the story of emigration when the evidence is scattered across the world. The genealogy element lets Irish-descended visitors look up their own family, which is the part people remember. Booking online saves 2 euros and teenagers pay 15.
places.what_ruined: There are no objects at all, which disappoints anyone expecting a conventional museum. Twenty-two euros is a lot for a screen-based experience in a city with several free national museums. Walk-up costs 2 euros more than booking ahead for exactly the same visit.
places.rating_rationale: Four because it does something genuinely difficult well: tell a diaspora story with almost no artefacts. Value is four, with online booking two euros cheaper and real family rates.
places.meta_description: EPIC costs 22 euros online or 24 on the day, with teenagers at 15. A fully digital museum about Irish emigration, and who it suits.

places.what_it_is: A fully digital museum in the vaults of the CHQ Building on Custom House Quay, telling the story of Irish emigration across twenty themed galleries, with an on-site genealogy service.
places.why_go: Because the Irish diaspora is one of the defining facts about the country and there is no artefact that can carry it. This is the place that takes the subject seriously rather than reducing it to famine and sentiment.
places.the_good: It makes a shapeless subject legible, and the genealogy service turns an abstract story into a personal one for anyone with Irish ancestry. Online booking is 2 euros cheaper, and teenage and child rates are genuinely reduced rather than token.
places.the_downsides: No collection and no objects, which is a real mismatch for some visitors at 22 euros. Dublin has free national museums a short walk away, which sharpens the comparison. The screens mean the experience is paced by the equipment rather than by you.
places.best_for: Anyone with Irish ancestry, particularly visitors from the United States, Canada or Australia; families with teenagers; and travellers interested in migration history generally.
places.skip_if: You want to look at objects, in which case the National Museum of Ireland is free and a few minutes away. Skip it too if you are on a tight budget in what is already an expensive city.
places.practical: Book online, which is 2 euros cheaper per adult than paying at the door. If you have Irish ancestry, allow extra time for the genealogy service rather than treating it as an add-on. The CHQ building has food and is a reasonable place to start or end a day on the docks.
places.tickets: Adults aged 18 to 64 pay 22.00 euros online or 24.00 on the day. Teenagers aged 13 to 17 pay 15.00 online or 16.00 on the day, with lower rates for children aged 6 to 12.
places.getting_there: The Luas red line stops at George's Dock, a minute away. It is about a fifteen-minute walk from O'Connell Bridge along the north quays.
places.location_context: Custom House Quay in the Docklands, east of the city centre on the north bank of the Liffey, in a redeveloped commercial district. The Jeanie Johnston famine ship replica and the Famine Memorial are both a short walk along the river.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the twenty galleries. Longer if you use the genealogy service.
places.accessibility: The museum is step-free throughout with lift access to the vault galleries, and publishes accessibility information for visitors.
places.verdict: A good museum doing a hard job, provided you know before you book that there is nothing in a case. Book online for the cheaper rate, and if you have Irish ancestry the genealogy service is what will make it worth 22 euros.

places.name: National Museum of Scotland
places.headline: Free Entry in a City That Charges for Almost Everything Else
places.body:
The National Museum of Scotland has free entry, with charges for some special exhibitions only. In a city where the castle, the underground tours and most of the Royal Mile attractions all charge, that single fact makes this the best-value few hours in Edinburgh.

The collection is unusually broad: Scottish history and archaeology in one wing, natural history, world cultures, science and technology in another, joined by a Victorian glass-roofed grand gallery that is worth standing in on its own.

The roof terrace is the part visitors miss. It is free, it is at the top of the building, and it gives a view over the Old Town rooftops to the castle that many people pay for elsewhere.
places.what_great: Free entry to a genuinely national-scale collection, which in Edinburgh is close to unique. The range means it works for almost anyone, including families on a wet afternoon. The roof terrace view over the Old Town costs nothing and is one of the best in the city.
places.what_ruined: It is large and the layout across old and new buildings confuses people, so first visits often involve backtracking. Special exhibitions are charged, which is a jolt inside a free museum. It is one of the busiest indoor spaces in Edinburgh during festival season and in bad weather.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. Entry is free, the collection ranges from Scottish history to natural science to technology, and the roof terrace gives one of the best free views in Edinburgh.
places.meta_description: The National Museum of Scotland has free entry, with charges only for some special exhibitions. Why it is the best-value few hours in Edinburgh.

places.why_go: Because it is free, comprehensive and central, and because the roof terrace gives a view of the castle and the Old Town that costs nothing. It is also the obvious answer to a wet Edinburgh afternoon, of which there are many.
places.the_good: Free entry, a collection broad enough to suit almost any interest, and a genuinely impressive Victorian grand gallery. The roof terrace is free and underused. Being free means a short visit is not a waste, so you can come back.
places.the_downsides: The building is a maze where the Victorian and modern halves meet, and the signage does not entirely solve it. Special exhibitions carry a charge. During the festival and on rainy days the central galleries get very busy.
places.best_for: Families, budget travellers, anyone caught in Edinburgh weather, and visitors who want one substantial cultural stop without adding to an already expensive trip.
places.skip_if: You have a single day in Edinburgh and want it to be about the city itself rather than a museum. The Old Town, Arthur's Seat and the walk down the Royal Mile are all free too.
places.practical: Go up to the roof terrace first, because most visitors never find it and it is quietest early. Enter from Chambers Street for the grand gallery rather than the modern side entrance. Since it costs nothing, treat it as two short visits rather than one exhausting one.
places.tickets: Entry is free. Some special exhibitions carry a charge.
places.getting_there: A short walk from Edinburgh Waverley station, or up from the Grassmarket. Numerous bus routes stop on nearby Nicolson Street and George IV Bridge.
places.location_context: Chambers Street in the Old Town, between the University of Edinburgh and the Royal Mile, with Greyfriars Kirkyard immediately behind and the Grassmarket downhill to the west.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours for a broad visit. An hour is enough for one wing plus the roof terrace, and costs nothing.
places.accessibility: The museum is step-free with lift access to all floors including the roof terrace, and publishes detailed accessibility information.
places.verdict: The single best-value attraction in Edinburgh, on the simple grounds that it is excellent and free. Start on the roof terrace, pick two wings rather than all of them, and come back if the weather turns again.

places.name: Ondine
places.headline: Thirty Pounds for Six Oysters, Two Minutes From the Royal Mile
places.body:
Ondine charges 30 pounds for six Cumbrae oysters with firecracker dressing and 35 pounds for crispy oysters with buffalo hot sauce, which tells you most of what you need to know about both the kitchen and the bill.

It is a seafood restaurant on the first floor of a building on George IV Bridge, a two-minute walk from the Royal Mile, and it has been the serious fish option in Edinburgh for well over a decade. Scottish shellfish is the point: langoustines, oysters, crab, and whatever the day boats landed.

Sit at the horseshoe crustacean bar rather than at a table. It is the same menu, the view is of the kitchen, and you can order two dishes without feeling you have under-committed.
places.what_great: Scottish shellfish handled by people who know what to do with it. A crustacean bar you can eat at properly rather than perch at. Close enough to the Royal Mile to be convenient and one floor up, so it is quiet.
places.what_ruined: Expensive, and shellfish prices climb quickly once you start adding. Being on the first floor makes it easy to walk past. It fills with the festival crowd in August, when booking becomes essential rather than advisable.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the best seafood cooking in the city. Five for safety in the Old Town. Three for value: thirty pounds for six oysters is a real price, and the quality is genuinely there.

places.what_it_is: A seafood restaurant on the first floor of a George IV Bridge building in Edinburgh's Old Town, cooking Scottish shellfish and day-boat fish around a horseshoe crustacean bar.
places.why_go: Because Scotland lands some of the best shellfish in Europe and most of it leaves the country. This is where it stays.
places.the_good: Excellent oysters and langoustines, a crustacean bar worth sitting at, a short menu that changes with the landings, and a first-floor room that stays calm.
places.the_downsides: Prices climb fast. Easy to miss from the street. Very busy through the August festival.
places.best_for: Anyone who likes shellfish, and anyone wanting one properly good meal without leaving the Old Town.

places.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
places.headline: Twenty-Two in Advance, Twenty-Six at the Door, and Mary Queen of Scots' Bedchamber
places.body:
The Palace of Holyroodhouse charges 22.00 pounds for an adult booking in advance and 26.00 pounds on the day. Young people aged 18 to 24 pay 14.00 in advance and 17.00 on the day, children aged 5 to 17 pay 11.00 and 13.00, disabled visitors pay the same rates as children, an access companion goes free and under 5s are free.

The palace is the King's official residence in Scotland, at the bottom of the Royal Mile with Arthur's Seat rising behind it. The part most people come for is the historic apartments: Mary Queen of Scots' chambers, including the small room where her secretary David Rizzio was murdered in 1566 in front of her while she was six months pregnant.

The ruined abbey in the grounds is the quieter surprise and is included in the ticket.
places.what_great: Mary Queen of Scots' apartments are the real thing rather than a reconstruction, and the Rizzio murder room lands harder in person than any retelling. The ruined abbey is included and is often empty. Booking ahead saves 4 pounds a head, and an access companion goes free.
places.what_ruined: Turning up without booking costs 4 pounds more per adult for exactly the same visit. The route is fixed and one-way, so you cannot linger where you want to. The palace closes to visitors entirely during royal visits, which is not always obvious when planning.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the historical apartments and the abbey ruins are genuinely strong, held back by a fixed route and a price that jumps if you do not book. Value is four: booking ahead saves 4 pounds and children pay 11.

places.what_it_is: The official residence in Scotland of the monarch, at the foot of the Royal Mile, comprising state apartments still used for official business, the sixteenth-century historic apartments of Mary Queen of Scots, and the ruins of Holyrood Abbey.
places.why_go: For Mary Queen of Scots' chambers and the Rizzio murder room, which is one of the few places in Britain where a famous violent episode happened in a room you can stand in.
places.the_good: Genuine sixteenth-century apartments rather than a reconstruction. The abbey ruins are included and usually quiet. Real concessions, with children at 11 pounds, free access companions and free entry for under 5s. Booking ahead saves 4 pounds.
places.the_downsides: Twenty-six pounds on the door is steep and entirely avoidable by booking. The route is fixed and paced by the crowd. Closures for royal visits can remove the option at short notice.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in Scottish or Tudor-era history, visitors walking the Royal Mile who want a substantial stop at the bottom of it, and families given the child rate.
places.skip_if: You have one paid attraction in your Edinburgh budget and have not done the castle. The castle is the more complete day. Skip it also if you cannot book ahead and object to paying 26 pounds.
places.practical: Book in advance, which saves 4 pounds per adult and guarantees entry. Check for royal visit closures before building a day around it. Do the Royal Mile downhill from the castle so this is your last stop, then walk into Holyrood Park for Arthur's Seat, which is free.
places.tickets: Adults pay 22.00 pounds in advance or 26.00 on the day. Young people aged 18 to 24 pay 14.00 and 17.00, children aged 5 to 17 pay 11.00 and 13.00, and disabled visitors pay 11.00 and 13.00. An access companion goes free and under 5s are free. A 2 pound transaction fee applies when pre-booking, and tickets can be converted to a one-year pass.
places.getting_there: At the foot of the Royal Mile, roughly a twenty-minute walk downhill from Edinburgh Castle. Lothian buses 6, 35 and 300 stop nearby, and Edinburgh Waverley is about fifteen minutes on foot.
places.location_context: The eastern end of the Old Town where the Royal Mile ends, with the Scottish Parliament directly opposite and Holyrood Park and Arthur's Seat immediately behind.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours including the abbey ruins and the gardens.
places.accessibility: Disabled visitors pay the child rate and an access companion enters free; the palace publishes detailed access information, and parts of the historic apartments are reached by stairs.
places.verdict: Worth it for Mary Queen of Scots' apartments, and clearly better value booked in advance than paid at the door. Make it the end of a Royal Mile walk and carry on into Holyrood Park afterwards, which costs nothing.

places.name: M+
places.headline: A Hundred and Ninety Hong Kong Dollars, and the Roof Garden Is Free
places.body:
M+ charges HKD 190 for a standard ticket and HKD 100 for concessions. It is closed on Mondays, and the ground space and roof garden remain free to enter without a ticket.

The museum opened in 2021 in a Herzog and de Meuron building on the West Kowloon waterfront, and it is the most serious attempt anywhere to build a collection of twentieth and twenty-first century visual culture from Asia. Design, architecture, moving image and ink painting are treated as equals rather than as departments beneath painting.

The view is the other half of the ticket. The building faces the whole of Hong Kong Island across the harbour, and the LED facade on the north side turns the museum itself into part of the skyline it looks at.
places.what_great: A genuinely new kind of collection, superbly installed, in one of the best museum buildings completed this century. The free roof garden and ground floor. Late Friday opening to 22:00.
places.what_ruined: A hundred and ninety dollars is high by Hong Kong museum standards, where the public museums charge a fraction of it. Session-based ticketing means you commit to a time slot. Closed Mondays.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a collection and building that are both world class. Five for safety in West Kowloon. Four for value: the price is fair internationally but steep next to Hong Kong's other museums.
places.meta_description: M+ in Hong Kong costs HKD 190 standard and HKD 100 concessions, closed Mondays. Asian visual culture in a Herzog and de Meuron building on the harbour.

places.what_it_is: A museum of twentieth and twenty-first century visual culture in the West Kowloon Cultural District, covering design, architecture, moving image and visual art with a particular focus on Asia.
places.why_go: Because no other museum has tried to write this history, and because the building and the harbour view would be worth the trip even if the collection were ordinary, which it is not.
places.the_good: An original and ambitious collection, exceptional installation, a free roof garden and ground floor, late Friday opening, and the best museum view in Asia.
places.the_downsides: Expensive relative to Hong Kong's public museums. Timed session tickets. Closed Mondays. The West Kowloon district around it is still filling in.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in design, film or contemporary art, and anyone who wants a view of the island skyline from the Kowloon side.
places.skip_if: You have one day and want Victoria Peak and the Star Ferry. Those are the stronger call for a first visit.
places.practical: Take a Friday night session and stay for the skyline after dark. The roof garden is free, so you can see the view without a ticket if the collection is not for you. Last entry to the galleries is thirty minutes before closing.
places.tickets: Standard HKD 190, concessions HKD 100. A two-person adult and child combo is HKD 250 and a three-person combo HKD 400. Tickets are sold by session: morning, afternoon and, on Fridays, night.
places.getting_there: MTR to Austin or Kowloon station, then a ten-minute walk through the West Kowloon Cultural District. The Star Ferry from Central lands at Tsim Sha Tsui, about twenty minutes away on foot.
places.location_context: The West Kowloon Cultural District, a reclaimed waterfront strip facing Hong Kong Island, alongside the Hong Kong Palace Museum and the Xiqu Centre.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours, plus time on the roof.
places.accessibility: Step-free throughout with lifts to all levels and accessible routes to the roof garden.
places.verdict: The best museum in Hong Kong and worth the hundred and ninety dollars. Take a Friday evening slot and finish on the free roof garden after dark.

places.name: Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory
places.headline: Sixty Zloty for the Factory, and It Is Not the Film You Remember
places.body:
Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory, a branch of the Museum of Krakow, charges 60 PLN for a normal ticket and 45 PLN reduced, with a family ticket for up to four people at 120 PLN. It opens Monday 10:00 to 15:00 and Tuesday to Sunday 9:00 to 20:00, and closes on the first Tuesday of each month.

The common misconception is that this is a Schindler museum. It is not. The permanent exhibition is about Krakow under German occupation between 1939 and 1945, and the factory is the setting rather than the subject. Schindler's office is preserved, but the exhibition around it belongs to the city, not to him.

That turns out to be the better museum. It is built as a walk-through of occupied Krakow, street by street, with reconstructed interiors, and it is one of the most effective wartime exhibitions in Europe precisely because it refuses to make the story about one rescuer.
places.what_great: An immersive, street-level reconstruction of an occupied city rather than a wall of text. Free admission on Mondays. Long opening hours in summer, to 20:00, which makes late afternoon a real option.
places.what_ruined: It is small, dark and extremely popular, and timed slots sell out days ahead in summer. Sixty zloty is at the top of the Krakow museum range. Visitors expecting the film's story leave disappointed, and the crowding in the narrow reconstructed corridors is genuinely uncomfortable at peak times.
places.rating_rationale: Five for one of the best-designed history exhibitions in central Europe. Five for safety in Zablocie. Four for value: 60 zloty is high locally, though free Mondays and the sheer quality of the exhibition offset it.

places.what_it_is: A branch of the Museum of Krakow in Oskar Schindler's former enamelware factory in Zablocie, holding a permanent exhibition on Krakow under German occupation from 1939 to 1945.
places.why_go: It is the most affecting account of the occupation anywhere in the city, and it does it by rebuilding the streets rather than by explaining them. Schindler's preserved office is a small part of a much larger story.
places.the_good: Exceptional exhibition design, a genuine sense of walking through the occupied city, free entry on Mondays, and English-language guided tours at set times.
places.the_downsides: Cramped, dark and heavily booked. Slots sell out in advance in summer. Expensive by Krakow standards. It is not the film, and people who come expecting it say so.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in the Second World War in central Europe, and anyone who wants to understand the city beyond the Old Town.
places.skip_if: You are travelling with young children, or you want the Schindler story specifically. Also skip it if you cannot book ahead in high season, because turning up is not a plan here.
places.practical: Book online in advance and bring original ID matching the booking, which is checked. Last entry is ninety minutes before closing. Monday is free but cannot be booked ahead, so queue early.
places.tickets: Normal 60 PLN, reduced 45 PLN, family ticket for up to four people 120 PLN. Free admission on Mondays, with tickets available only at the branch and in limited numbers.
places.getting_there: Tram to Plac Bohaterow Getta then a ten-minute walk over the river into Zablocie, or a twenty-five-minute walk from the Old Town through Kazimierz.
places.location_context: Zablocie, a post-industrial district across the Vistula from Kazimierz, now half warehouses and half new apartment blocks. The MOCAK contemporary art museum is next door.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours. The route is one way and takes as long as it takes.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve the exhibition levels, though the reconstructed corridors are narrow and get congested.
places.verdict: The best museum in Krakow and worth the sixty zloty, as long as you book ahead and arrive knowing it is about the city rather than about Schindler.

places.name: Kinkaku-ji
places.headline: Five Hundred Yen for One of the Best Views in Japan, and You Cannot Linger
places.body:
Kinkaku-ji is the rare famous thing that is not overpriced. General admission is 500 yen, primary and middle school students pay 300 yen, and the temple is open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. all year round. Against Kyoto's 2026 cost of visiting, where the top band of the city lodging tax is 10,000 yen per person per night, a 500 yen ticket to the Golden Pavilion is close to the best value in the city.

What the price does not buy is time with it. The route through the grounds is a one-way loop and the pavilion is viewed from across the Mirror Pond rather than entered. The honest description is a walk of twenty to thirty minutes with one spectacular sightline near the start, which is where every other visitor is also standing.

Plan it as one stop rather than the day. The 9:00 opening is the single best lever you have.
places.what_great: Five hundred yen, open every day of the year, and no reservation system to navigate. The gold leaf reflected in the Mirror Pond is a genuinely singular sight and the grounds are immaculately kept. For a city that has spent 2026 adding costs to visitors, this is one of the few headline attractions that has not moved its price out of reach.
places.what_ruined: You cannot go inside the pavilion, and the loop is one-way, so if the main viewpoint is packed you cannot circle back and wait it out. The whole visit is short enough that people who cross the city for it alone often feel shortchanged. It is in the far north-west, so it costs you a bus ride each way.
places.rating_rationale: Four rather than five because the visit is short, one-way and viewed at a distance, which is a real limitation rather than a matter of taste. Value is five: 500 yen is exceptional for a site of this stature in a city that has spent 2026 raising the cost of visiting.
places.meta_description: Kinkaku-ji costs 500 yen and opens 9:00 to 17:00 all year. Why the visit is shorter than you expect and how to time it properly.

places.what_it_is: A Zen temple in north-west Kyoto whose top two floors are covered in gold leaf, set on a pond in a formal garden. The current pavilion is a 1955 reconstruction after the original was destroyed by arson in 1950.
places.why_go: For one specific view: the gold pavilion reflected in the Mirror Pond, which is among the most recognisable images in Japan and considerably better in person than in photographs.
places.the_good: Five hundred yen, open all year, no advance booking required. The grounds are meticulously maintained and the entrance ticket is issued as a paper charm, which is a small thing people keep. In a city that has been raising visitor costs steadily, this price has not moved.
places.the_downsides: The pavilion cannot be entered and the route is one-way, so a crowded viewpoint cannot be waited out. The visit is short for the journey involved. Mid-afternoon is markedly busier than opening time for exactly the same 500 yen.
places.best_for: First-time visitors to Kyoto, anyone on a budget given the price, and photographers who can be at the gate for opening.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Kyoto and want depth rather than an icon, in which case Fushimi Inari or the Higashiyama temples give you considerably more time on your feet for your money.
places.practical: Be there at 9:00. The pond view faces the crowd bottleneck and the pavilion catches morning light well. Combine it with Ryoan-ji and Ninna-ji, which are close by on the same side of the city, otherwise you are spending most of the trip on a bus for a half-hour visit.
places.tickets: General admission is 500 yen and primary and middle school students pay 300 yen. There is no advance reservation system; tickets are bought at the gate. Open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., all year round.
places.getting_there: Kyoto City Bus 101 or 205 from Kyoto Station to Kinkakuji-michi. Note that Kyoto abolished the bus-only day pass to keep tourists off local routes, so price the individual fares rather than assuming a pass.
places.location_context: Kita ward, in the far north-west of Kyoto, well away from the Higashiyama temple belt on the other side of the city. Ryoan-ji and Ninna-ji are both nearby and are the natural pairings.
places.time_needed: Thirty to forty-five minutes on site. Budget an hour and a half to two hours including the bus each way from central Kyoto.
places.verdict: Excellent value and genuinely worth seeing, provided you treat it as one stop on a north-west Kyoto morning rather than a destination in itself. Arrive at opening and pair it with Ryoan-ji.

places.name: Nijo Castle
places.headline: Eight Hundred Yen for the Floors That Were Built to Betray You
places.body:
Nijo Castle charges 800 yen for a castle admission ticket, with 400 yen for junior and senior high school students and 300 yen for elementary school students. Entry is free of charge for those under elementary school age.

What makes it worth the trip is the Ninomaru Palace, and specifically its floors. They are built to chirp underfoot, the so-called nightingale floors, as a security measure against anyone approaching unheard. You walk the whole palace on them, and the sound follows you room to room.

The painted screens inside are originals or high-quality reproductions depending on the room, and the rooms themselves are arranged by rank, so the further in you get the more restricted the access historically was. It is the clearest surviving illustration of how Tokugawa power was staged.
places.what_great: Eight hundred yen for a UNESCO World Heritage site with intact palace interiors is exceptional value, particularly in a city that put its lodging tax up to 10,000 yen a night at the top band in 2026. The nightingale floors are a genuine physical experience rather than a display, and the grounds and gardens are included.
places.what_ruined: The Ninomaru Palace interior is a single one-way route in socks with no photography permitted, so it moves at the pace of the group. The Honmaru Palace requires a separate advance reservation and its own ticket. Coach tours arrive in waves and the palace corridors do not absorb them well.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. The nightingale floors and the Ninomaru palace interiors are unlike anything else in Kyoto, and at 800 yen it is one of the best-value major sites in a city that has been raising prices everywhere else.
places.meta_description: Nijo Castle costs 800 yen for adults and 400 for high school students. The nightingale floors, the palace interiors, and when to go.

places.what_it_is: A flatland castle in central Kyoto built by the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603, comprising the Ninomaru Palace with its nightingale floors and painted screens, the separately ticketed Honmaru Palace, and extensive gardens. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage listing.
places.why_go: For the Ninomaru Palace, which is one of the few places you can walk through intact shogunate-era state rooms, and for the floors, which are an engineering answer to assassination that you experience with your feet.
places.the_good: Eight hundred yen for a World Heritage site with intact interiors. The nightingale floors work exactly as described. School-age rates are genuinely cheap and under-school-age children are free. The gardens are included and are worth the extra twenty minutes.
places.the_downsides: The palace route is one-way, in socks, with no photography, and you move at the speed of whoever is in front of you. The Honmaru Palace is a separate ticket needing advance reservation. Tour coaches concentrate through the middle of the day.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in Japanese history or architecture, families given the cheap child rates, and travellers who want a major Kyoto site that has not priced itself out of reach.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Kyoto and want temples and gardens rather than political history, in which case Fushimi Inari and the Higashiyama walk give you more. Skip the Honmaru add-on unless you have booked it in advance.
places.practical: Go at opening or in the last ninety minutes to miss the coach groups. Wear socks you are happy to walk a palace in, since shoes come off for the Ninomaru route. If you want the Honmaru Palace, reserve it in advance; it cannot be added on arrival.
places.tickets: A castle admission ticket is 800 yen, with 400 yen for junior and senior high school students and 300 yen for elementary school students. Entry is free of charge for those under elementary school age. A combined castle and Ninomaru palace ticket is sold at a higher price, and the Honmaru Palace requires a separate advance reservation.
places.getting_there: Nijojo-mae station on the Tozai subway line is directly outside. City buses 9, 12, 50 and 101 stop at Nijojo-mae. Note that Kyoto abolished the bus-only day pass, so price individual fares.
places.location_context: Nakagyo ward, central Kyoto, west of the Imperial Palace and north of the Shijo shopping district. Unlike the Higashiyama temple belt on the eastern hills, this is flat central city, so it combines easily with the Imperial Palace or Nishiki Market.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes for the Ninomaru Palace and the main gardens. Two hours if you walk the full grounds.
places.accessibility: The grounds are largely flat, but the Ninomaru Palace route involves removing shoes and walking wooden corridors with steps, which limits access.
places.verdict: The best-value major site in Kyoto and the one that best explains how the country was actually governed. Go early, take the gardens as well as the palace, and reserve the Honmaru separately if you want it.

places.name: Central
places.headline: Two Services a Day, and Both of Them Book Out Months Ahead
places.body:
Central serves Monday to Saturday, lunch from 12:45 to 13:30 and dinner from 19:00 to 20:30. Those windows are seating times, not opening hours: you arrive inside them or you do not eat.

The restaurant is organised by altitude. Each course comes from a specific elevation of Peru, from below sea level to high Andes, and the menu is presented as a vertical cross-section of the country. It is a conceit that could be unbearable and is not, because the ingredients genuinely do not appear anywhere else.

It has spent years at or near the top of the World's 50 Best list, which means reservations open months ahead and close quickly.
places.what_great: A tasting menu organised around Peruvian ecosystems, using ingredients that essentially never leave the country. Two tightly controlled services a day, so nothing is rushed. In Barranco, which is the best neighbourhood in Lima to be in anyway.
places.what_ruined: Booking months in advance is not optional. The seating windows are narrow and fixed. It is very expensive by any standard and by Peruvian standards it is extraordinary. The altitude framing can feel like a lecture if you are not in the mood.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a restaurant doing something no one else is attempting. Four for safety in Barranco, which is fine with normal city sense. Three for value: it is a major expense, defensible once.

places.what_it_is: A tasting-menu restaurant in Barranco, Lima, whose courses are organised by the altitude their ingredients come from, spanning Peruvian ecosystems from the ocean floor to the high Andes.
places.why_go: For ingredients that do not travel and a structure that teaches you something about the country while you eat. It is the most ambitious restaurant in South America and it earns the description.
places.the_good: An idea followed through completely, ingredients unavailable anywhere else, tightly run services, and a Barranco setting worth arriving early for.
places.the_downsides: Months-ahead booking. Narrow fixed seatings. Very expensive. The concept is delivered with some ceremony.
places.best_for: Anyone building a trip around food, and anyone curious about Peru beyond ceviche and pisco sours.
places.skip_if: You cannot book far ahead, or you would rather eat at five cevicherias for the same money, which is a completely defensible choice in Lima.
places.practical: Book months in advance, and take lunch if you would rather have the afternoon than the evening. Arrive inside the seating window, because it is enforced. Walk Barranco before or after; it is the reason to be in that part of the city.
places.tickets: Tasting menu with optional pairings, booked online. Services are Monday to Saturday only, lunch 12:45 to 13:30 and dinner 19:00 to 20:30.
places.getting_there: A taxi from Miraflores takes about ten minutes and from central Lima about thirty. Use an app taxi rather than the street.
places.location_context: Barranco, the coastal bohemian district south of Miraflores, with cliffs over the Pacific, street art and the best bar scene in the city.
places.time_needed: Three hours.
places.verdict: Book months ahead or do not plan on it. The most interesting meal in South America, and lunch is the easier service to get.

places.name: Museo Larco
places.headline: Fifty Soles for Forty-Five Thousand Pots and an Open Storeroom
places.body:
Museo Larco charges 50 soles for general admission, 35 soles for over-60s, 25 soles for students and children aged 9 to 17, and 1 sol for children aged 3 to 8. Children under 3 enter free.

The collection is pre-Columbian, mostly Moche, and it is enormous. What makes the museum unusual is that it does not hide the rest: the visible storeroom holds around 45,000 catalogued pieces on open shelves, rack after rack, which conveys the scale of Peruvian ceramic production in a way no curated selection can.

It occupies an eighteenth-century mansion built on a seventh-century pyramid in Pueblo Libre, surrounded by gardens, and the restaurant on the terrace is one of the better meals in Lima.
places.what_great: The visible storeroom, which almost no museum anywhere allows. Superb Moche portrait vessels and metalwork. Gardens, a genuinely good restaurant, and a building worth seeing on its own.
places.what_ruined: Fifty soles is at the top of the Lima museum range. Pueblo Libre is a taxi ride from Miraflores and Barranco where most visitors stay. The erotic ceramics gallery is signposted in a way that guarantees crowds.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the collection and the storeroom together. Four for safety: Pueblo Libre is fine but take a registered taxi rather than walking in after dark. Four for value: fifty soles is fair for what it holds.

places.what_it_is: A private museum of pre-Columbian art in Pueblo Libre, Lima, in an eighteenth-century mansion built over a pre-Columbian pyramid, holding one of the largest collections of Moche ceramics in the world.
places.why_go: For the visible storeroom. Seeing 45,000 pieces on open racks changes what you understand about how much of this material exists, and no photograph of a museum case does that.
places.the_good: An outstanding Moche collection, the open storeroom, the gold and silver gallery, gardens, and a terrace restaurant that is a destination in itself.
places.the_downsides: Expensive for Lima. Away from the tourist districts. The erotic gallery draws a disproportionate share of the crowd and the giggling.
places.best_for: Anyone going to Machu Picchu, who should come here first, and anyone interested in ceramics or ancient art.
places.skip_if: You are in Lima for one night between flights. In that case eat in Miraflores instead.
places.practical: Go before Cusco, not after: the context makes the sites far more legible. Book a time slot online. Leave time for the storeroom, which people rush and should not.
places.tickets: General admission 50.00 soles, over-60s 35.00 soles, students and 9 to 17 year olds 25.00 soles, children 3 to 8 pay 1.00 sol, under-3s free. Online purchase requires choosing a time slot.
places.getting_there: A fifteen to twenty minute taxi from Miraflores. There is no convenient metro; use a registered app taxi rather than the street.
places.location_context: Pueblo Libre, a quiet residential district between the centre and the coast, away from the tourist strip and pleasant in daylight.
places.time_needed: Two hours, including the storeroom.
places.accessibility: Ramps and step-free routes serve the main galleries, though the historic mansion has some tight passages.
places.verdict: Go before you fly to Cusco. Fifty soles for the best pre-Columbian collection in Peru, and the open storeroom is the thing you will still be describing to people afterwards.

places.name: Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
places.headline: Eighteen Euros for One Man's Astonishing Shopping
places.body:
The Calouste Gulbenkian Museum charges 18.00 euros for an all-inclusive ticket, 16.00 euros for the museum and CAM together, and 12.00 euros for CAM alone. It opens 10:00 to 18:00, until 21:00 on Saturdays, and is closed on Tuesdays.

Gulbenkian was an Armenian oil magnate who took five per cent of Iraqi petroleum in kind and spent it on whatever he liked for fifty years. The result is one of the best private collections ever assembled: Egyptian sculpture, Persian carpets, Chinese porcelain, Rembrandt, Rubens, Monet, and a room of Rene Lalique jewellery that is worth the ticket on its own.

The garden around it is one of the great modernist landscapes in Europe, free to enter, and full of Lisbon residents doing nothing in particular.
places.what_great: A collection with no weak rooms, in a building that is a masterpiece of 1960s museum design. The Lalique room. A free garden that is a genuine public space. Saturday opening to 21:00.
places.what_ruined: Eighteen euros is high for Lisbon, and the ticket tiers are confusing: the museum, the modern art centre and the combinations all cost different amounts. Closed Tuesdays. It is a metro ride from the tourist centre, which puts people off.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a collection and a building that are both exceptional. Five for safety in a quiet residential district. Four for value: excellent, but eighteen euros is a Lisbon premium and the ticket structure is needlessly complicated.
places.meta_description: The Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon costs 18 euros all inclusive, 16 with CAM, and closes Tuesdays. One oil magnate's fifty years of collecting.

places.what_it_is: The museum of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in Avenidas Novas, holding the founder's private collection of ancient, Islamic, Asian and European art, alongside the CAM modern art centre and a large public garden.
places.why_go: For range and quality that no other museum in Portugal comes near, and for the Lalique jewellery, which is the finest collection of it anywhere.
places.the_good: Egyptian, Islamic, Chinese and European rooms all strong. The Lalique collection. A superb modernist building. A free garden. Late Saturday opening. Free entry to exhibitions on Sundays from 14:00.
places.the_downsides: Confusing ticket tiers. Closed Tuesdays. Away from the tourist centre. Eighteen euros is steep for the city.
places.best_for: Anyone who likes decorative arts, and anyone staying in Lisbon long enough to leave Baixa and Belem behind.
places.skip_if: You have two days and have not yet seen Belem. The Jeronimos monastery has the stronger claim on a short trip.
places.practical: Decide which ticket you want before you get to the desk. Saturday evening is the calmest slot. The garden is free, so it works as a break in the middle rather than a separate trip.

places.getting_there: Metro to Sao Sebastiao or Praca de Espanha, both a few minutes' walk. It is about fifteen minutes by metro from Baixa.
places.location_context: Avenidas Novas, a twentieth-century residential and office district north of the centre, quiet and green and largely free of tourists.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours for the founder's collection, longer with CAM and the garden.
places.accessibility: Step-free throughout with lifts, and the garden paths are largely level.
places.verdict: The best museum in Portugal. Work out which ticket you want before you arrive, go late on a Saturday, and give the free garden half an hour of its own.

places.name: Oceanario de Lisboa
places.headline: Twenty-Nine Euros at Opening, Twenty-Seven at Midday, and Under-Threes Free
places.body:
The Oceanario prices by time slot, which is unusual and worth understanding before you book. For the 10 am to 11:30 am slot, ages 0 to 2 are free, 3 to 12 year olds pay 17 euros, 13 to 64 year olds pay 29 euros and over-65s pay 19 euros. From 12 pm to 3:30 pm the same tiers drop to 16, 27 and 18 euros.

So the busiest slot is also the most expensive one, and going a couple of hours later is both cheaper and quieter. That is the opposite of how most attractions work and most visitors do not notice it.

The building itself sits out in the marina at Parque das Nacoes, reached by a walkway over the water. The design centres on one enormous tank, viewed from two levels, with four separate habitat displays arranged around it so that the central ocean is always visible through them. It reads as one continuous ocean rather than a series of boxes, and it is the reason this aquarium is regularly rated the best in Europe.
places.what_great: The central-tank design is genuinely clever and holds attention far longer than a conventional aquarium. Under-3s go free and the midday slot is 2 euros cheaper per adult than the opening one. Parque das Nacoes around it is pleasant, modern and easy to walk with children.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-nine euros for an adult at the opening slot makes a family visit expensive. It is out at Parque das Nacoes, well away from central Lisbon, so it costs a metro trip each way. Weekends and school holidays are very busy regardless of which slot you pick.
places.rating_rationale: Five because it is one of the best-designed public aquariums in the world and the central tank genuinely works. Value is four: 29 euros is a lot for a family, though the tiered time slots and free under-threes soften it.
places.meta_description: The Oceanario de Lisboa charges 29 euros for adults at opening, 27 midday, with under-3s free and children 3-12 at 17 euros.

places.what_it_is: A public aquarium in the Parque das Nacoes marina, built for Expo 98, arranged around a single very large central tank with four habitat zones surrounding it representing the North Atlantic, Antarctic, Pacific and Indian Ocean coasts.
places.why_go: For the central tank, which is visible from every surrounding habitat so the whole building reads as one ocean rather than a corridor of glass boxes. It is a genuinely better idea than most aquariums manage.
places.the_good: Outstanding design that keeps people looking for far longer than usual. Free entry for under-3s and a real discount for over-65s. Cheaper midday slots. The walk out over the water to the building is a good start to a visit.
places.the_downsides: Twenty-nine euros an adult in the opening slot, and the family total mounts quickly. It is a long way from the historic centre. It is one of the busiest attractions in Lisbon at weekends and in school holidays.
places.best_for: Families, anyone travelling with children, and visitors interested in design and architecture as much as marine life.
places.skip_if: You have two days in Lisbon and have not seen Belem or Alfama. Those are the city. This is a very good aquarium that happens to be in Lisbon rather than a reason to come.
places.practical: Book the 12 pm to 3:30 pm slot rather than the opening one: it is 2 euros cheaper per adult and less crowded. Allow an hour each way for travel from the centre. Combine it with Parque das Nacoes itself, which is free to walk and has the cable car along the waterfront.
places.tickets: Time-slot pricing. For 10 am to 11:30 am: 0 to 2 free, 3 to 12 at 17 euros, 13 to 64 at 29 euros, over-65s at 19 euros. For 12 pm to 3:30 pm: 16, 27 and 18 euros for the same tiers, with under-3s still free.
places.getting_there: Oriente station on Metro line 3, served also by mainline and suburban trains, then about ten minutes on foot through Parque das Nacoes.
places.location_context: Parque das Nacoes in the far north-east of Lisbon, the redeveloped Expo 98 site on the Tagus, which is modern, spacious and entirely unlike the old city. The Vasco da Gama bridge and the waterfront cable car are both here.
places.time_needed: Two hours inside. Allow half a day including travel from central Lisbon.
places.accessibility: The building is step-free throughout with lifts between the two viewing levels, and the approach walkway is level.
places.verdict: The best aquarium in Europe and worth the trip out, provided you book the midday slot rather than the opening one. It is a second-day Lisbon attraction, not a substitute for Belem or the old city.

places.name: Pasteis de Belem
places.headline: One Euro Sixty for the Custard Tart Everyone Else Is Copying
places.body:
Pasteis de Belem sells its pastel de nata at 1.60 euros each and 9.60 euros for a packet of six. There is no reservation and no way to skip the queue except to sit down.

This is the original. The recipe came from the Jeronimos monastery next door in 1837, it has not left the family since, and the shop still makes them behind a door only a handful of people are allowed through. Everywhere else in Portugal sells a pastel de nata; this is the one they are all approximating.

The queue outside is for takeaway. The rooms inside, which run back much further than the frontage suggests, are usually quicker and let you eat them at the correct temperature, which is straight out of the oven, dusted with cinnamon.
places.what_great: One euro sixty for something genuinely singular. Warm from the oven, which is a different object from the cold ones sold elsewhere. The tiled back rooms seat hundreds and most tourists never look past the takeaway queue.
places.what_ruined: The takeaway queue is long and visible and pulls people into it unnecessarily. It is in Belem, a tram ride from the centre, and the whole area is heaving by mid-morning. A packet of six is a commitment.
places.rating_rationale: Five all round. It is the original, it costs 1.60 euros, and the difference between one of these warm and a supermarket nata is not subtle.
places.meta_description: Pasteis de Belem in Lisbon sells its custard tarts at 1.60 euros each, 9.60 for six. Skip the takeaway queue and sit in the back rooms instead.

places.what_it_is: The pastry shop in Belem that has made the original pastel de nata to the Jeronimos monastery recipe since 1837, with a takeaway counter and a warren of tiled dining rooms behind it.
places.why_go: Because every other custard tart in the world is a copy of this one, and because eating them warm rather than cold is the entire point and is only reliably possible here.
places.the_good: The tarts themselves, the price, the enormous tiled back rooms, and the fact that a 190-year-old recipe is still being made on the premises rather than shipped in.
places.the_downsides: Crowds. A queue that is longer than it needs to be because people join it by default. Belem is a trip in itself. Table service can be brisk to the point of curt.
places.best_for: Everyone, honestly, and particularly anyone combining it with the Jeronimos monastery two minutes away.
places.skip_if: You have no interest in pastry and no plans in Belem. Otherwise there is no argument for skipping it.
places.practical: Ignore the takeaway queue and walk inside to the back rooms, which are much larger than they look and usually faster. Order them warm, add cinnamon and icing sugar from the shakers on the table, and eat them immediately.
places.tickets: 1.60 euros for a single pastel, 9.60 euros for a packet of six. No reservations; walk in and sit down.
places.getting_there: Tram 15E from Praca da Figueira to Belem, about twenty-five minutes, or the train from Cais do Sodre to Belem station.
places.location_context: Rua de Belem, directly across from the Jeronimos monastery and a few minutes from the Belem tower and the Coach Museum.
places.time_needed: Twenty minutes standing, forty-five if you sit.
places.verdict: The best 1.60 euros in Lisbon. Walk past the queue, sit in the back, and eat them warm.

places.name: Pestana Palace Lisboa
places.headline: A Hundred and Ninety Rooms Inside a Listed National Monument
places.body:
Pestana Palace Lisboa has 190 rooms and suites. Check-in is from 3:00 p.m. and check-out until 12:00 p.m. Nightly rates are not published as a fixed figure and move with season and availability, so treat the current rate as something to request rather than something we can quote.

The hotel is a nineteenth-century palace in Alcantara, classified as a national monument, with a domed entrance hall, a monumental staircase and French-style gardens that are part of the listing. There is a swimming pool, the Casa do Lago restaurant and a spa in the grounds.

It is a genuine palace rather than a hotel styled as one, which is the distinction that matters here and the reason the public rooms are worth walking through even if you are not staying.
places.what_great: An actual listed palace with gardens, not a pastiche. A hundred and ninety rooms, so it has the staffing of a full resort. A pool and spa in the grounds, which almost nothing central in Lisbon offers.
places.what_ruined: Alcantara is west of the centre, so everything is a taxi or a tram ride. The scale means it can feel more like a resort than a city hotel. No published rate card, so budgeting means asking.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a listed palace running properly as a hotel. Five for safety in Alcantara. Four for value: less central than the price implies, and you get gardens and a pool that no central hotel can match.

places.what_it_is: A 190-room hotel in a nineteenth-century palace in Alcantara, Lisbon, classified as a national monument, with French-style gardens, a swimming pool and a spa.
places.why_go: Because it is a real palace with the listing to prove it, and because the gardens and pool give you somewhere to be in the afternoon that central Lisbon hotels cannot offer.
places.the_good: A listed nineteenth-century palace, gardens that form part of the monument, a pool, a spa, and the staffing that 190 rooms supports.
places.the_downsides: West of the centre, so you commute in. Resort-scale rather than intimate. No published rates.
places.best_for: Travelers who want space and grounds rather than a central address, and anyone with a car or an unhurried itinerary.
places.skip_if: You want to walk to Baixa and Alfama from your door. Stay in Chiado or Baixa instead.
places.practical: Ask for a room facing the gardens. Walk the public rooms and the staircase whether or not your room looks onto them. Budget for taxis into the centre, or use the tram from Alcantara.

places.location_context: Alcantara, west of the centre between Belem and the bridge, a former industrial district now holding LX Factory and the docks nightlife.
places.time_needed: Three nights, given the distance from the centre.
places.verdict: A genuine palace with gardens and a pool, at the cost of a central address. Ask for a garden-facing room and request the rate directly.

places.name: Buckingham Palace State Rooms
places.headline: Thirty-Three Pounds in Advance, Thirty-Seven on the Day, and One Pound on Universal Credit
places.body:
The State Rooms at Buckingham Palace charge 33.00 pounds for an adult booking in advance and 37.00 pounds on the day. Young people aged 18 to 24 pay 21.50 in advance and 24.50 on the day.

The detail worth knowing, and one that is not widely advertised, is that 1 pound tickets are available to people on Universal Credit and other named UK benefits. That is a serious concession on an otherwise expensive ticket and it applies to the same visit.

The State Rooms are the working ceremonial heart of the palace, used for official entertaining, and they are open to visitors only during limited periods of the year. That scarcity is part of what you are paying for.
places.what_great: The rooms are genuinely on the scale the building implies, and they are the ones actually used for state occasions rather than a reconstruction. Booking in advance saves 4 pounds a head. The 1 pound benefits ticket is a real and unusually generous concession.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-three pounds is expensive and 37 on the day punishes spontaneity. Opening is seasonal, so the visit is unavailable for much of the year. The route is fixed and busy, and photography is restricted inside the State Rooms.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the State Rooms are genuinely grand and open only part of the year, which makes the visit feel earned. Value is three: 33 pounds in advance is a lot, and rises to 37 if you turn up without booking.

places.what_it_is: The nineteen State Rooms at Buckingham Palace, the ceremonial rooms used for official entertaining by the monarch, opened to visitors during limited periods of the year.
places.why_go: Because these are the rooms actually used for state occasions, at a scale and level of finish that photographs flatten. The Throne Room and the Picture Gallery in particular are hard to compare to anything else open to the public in London.
places.the_good: Genuine ceremonial interiors rather than a museum reconstruction, a meaningful advance-booking saving of 4 pounds a head, and a 1 pound ticket for visitors on Universal Credit and other named UK benefits. Seasonal opening keeps the visit feeling like an event.
places.the_downsides: At 33 pounds in advance and 37 on the day this is one of the most expensive tickets in London. Opening is limited to parts of the year, so most visitors cannot go at all. The route is fixed, crowded and photography-restricted.
places.best_for: Visitors with an interest in the monarchy or in interiors, anyone in London during the opening season who has budgeted for one major paid attraction, and UK benefit claimants who qualify for the 1 pound ticket.
places.skip_if: You are visiting outside the opening season, in which case the question is settled for you. Skip it too if you are choosing between this and Westminster Abbey or St Paul's on a limited budget, since all three are expensive and this is the most so.
places.practical: Book in advance rather than paying on the day, which saves 4 pounds per adult and guarantees entry. Check the opening dates before building a trip around it. If you or anyone in your party receives Universal Credit or another named UK benefit, check the 1 pound ticket before booking anything else.

places.getting_there: Green Park on the Jubilee, Piccadilly and Victoria lines, St James's Park on the Circle and District lines, and Victoria station are all within a short walk.

places.time_needed: Two to two and a half hours for the State Rooms with the audio guide, longer if a garden route is included in your ticket.
