Step-free access has to be pre-booked through the specialist sales team, as does accessible parking, which needs at least three full working days' notice. A free access companion ticket can be booked online.

places.name: Natural History Museum
places.headline: Free, Enormous, and Best Visited in the Last Two Hours of the Day
places.body:
The Natural History Museum is free, and that single fact changes how you should plan it. There is no ticket to justify, so there is no reason to try to see everything, and no reason not to come twice.

The museum offers free entry tickets you can book in advance, which is the practical lever: booked ticket holders skip the general queue. On a wet weekend in school holidays that queue is the entire difference between a good visit and an hour on the pavement.

The building itself, Waterhouse's terracotta cathedral of a museum, is the thing many people remember longest. The main hall is worth ten minutes and is where almost everybody stalls; the galleries beyond it empty out considerably.
places.what_great: It costs nothing, which makes a short focused visit completely guilt-free. Free entry tickets let you skip the queue. The architecture is a genuine attraction in its own right, and the mineral and meteorite galleries are consistently quiet while the crowd is downstairs.
places.what_ruined: The queue without a booked ticket can be long and is entirely avoidable, which makes it more annoying. The main hall and the dinosaur gallery are the two most crowded rooms in the museum and are the two everybody heads for first. Paid special exhibitions sit inside a free museum, which is a jarring transition.
places.rating_rationale: Five across the board. It is free, the building alone justifies the trip, and the only real cost is crowding, which is a scheduling problem rather than a value problem.
places.meta_description: The Natural History Museum is free to enter, and free timed tickets exist to skip the queue. How to visit it without spending your day in the main hall.

places.what_it_is: A national museum of natural history in South Kensington, housed in an 1881 Waterhouse building, covering life and earth sciences from dinosaurs and mammals to minerals, meteorites and human origins.
places.why_go: Because it is one of the great free museums anywhere, and because the building is as much the point as the collection. Very few museums of this quality cost nothing to enter.
places.the_good: Free entry, free bookable tickets that bypass the queue, and enough range that a repeat visit finds new things. Members get free entry to the paid exhibitions and can skip queues. The quieter upper galleries are genuinely peaceful even on busy days.
places.the_downsides: Without a booked ticket the entry queue can be substantial. The main hall and dinosaurs are heavily congested, which shapes many people's whole impression. Special exhibitions are ticketed separately inside an otherwise free museum.
places.best_for: Families, anyone in London on a budget, repeat visitors who can treat it as a one-hour stop, and people who care about Victorian architecture as much as about the collection.
places.skip_if: You have one day in London and no particular interest in natural history. It is a superb museum but it is not the thing that makes London distinctive, and the Victoria and Albert next door may suit you better.
places.practical: Book a free entry ticket in advance and go straight past the main hall, coming back to it later when the entry surge has moved on. The last two hours of the day are markedly calmer than the middle. South Kensington station connects by tunnel, which matters in the rain.
places.tickets: General admission is free. Free entry tickets can be booked in advance and let you skip the queue. Special exhibitions are ticketed separately, and members get free entry to them.
places.getting_there: South Kensington on the Circle, District and Piccadilly lines, with a pedestrian tunnel running from the station to the museums, which is the sensible route in bad weather.
places.location_context: South Kensington, on Exhibition Road alongside the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Science Museum. Three major free museums sit within a few minutes of each other, which makes this the highest-value square mile in London for anyone not spending money.
places.time_needed: Two hours is a good visit. Ninety minutes is enough if you pick two galleries. Because it is free there is no penalty in leaving early and returning another day.
places.accessibility: Step-free access is available and the museum publishes detailed access information; the tunnel route from South Kensington station avoids the street crossing entirely.
places.verdict: One of the best-value attractions in Europe by the simple measure that it costs nothing and is world class. Book the free ticket, skip the main hall crush, and treat it as two short visits rather than one long one.

places.name: Rules
places.headline: Twelve Pounds for Soup in the Oldest Restaurant in London
places.body:
Rules charges 5.75 pounds each for Poole rock oysters and 11.95 pounds for chilled leek and potato soup, which places it firmly in the expensive-but-not-absurd bracket for central London.

It opened in 1798 and has never moved or closed, which makes it the oldest restaurant in London. The dining rooms are dark red, hung floor to ceiling with prints, cartoons and taxidermy, and they look exactly like the idea of an English restaurant that England exports.

The kitchen is serious about game, which is the reason to come between August and January: grouse, partridge, woodcock and venison from the restaurant's own estate in the Pennines. Order that, not the steak.
places.what_great: Two and a quarter centuries in the same rooms, and they look it in the best way. Genuinely good game from their own estate in season. A bar upstairs that most diners never find.
places.what_ruined: Prices are high for what is fundamentally traditional cooking. The dining room is dark and closely packed. It is in Covent Garden, so the surrounding streets are a tourist crush from noon onwards, and the dress code is stricter than most visitors expect.
places.rating_rationale: Four for the room and the game cookery, which are both genuinely good. Five for safety. Three for value: you are paying a premium for the history, and that is a fair trade only if the history is what you came for.
places.meta_description: Rules in London, open since 1798, charges 5.75 for oysters and 11.95 for soup. Come for the game between August and January, not the steak.

places.what_it_is: London's oldest restaurant, open in Covent Garden since 1798, serving traditional British cooking with a particular emphasis on game from its own estate in the Pennines.
places.why_go: For game, in season, cooked by people who have been doing it longer than anyone else, in a room that has been doing it since before Trafalgar.
places.the_good: Estate game from August to January, a dining room that is a genuine period piece rather than a reconstruction, and an upstairs cocktail bar that is far quieter than the restaurant.
places.the_downsides: Expensive for traditional cooking. Cramped and dark. Covent Garden crowds outside. A dress code that turns people away at the door.
places.best_for: Anyone who wants game, and anyone who wants one properly old-fashioned English meal without it being a theme restaurant.
places.skip_if: You are vegetarian, or you would rather eat something modern. Both are entirely reasonable positions here.
places.practical: Book, and go in game season if you can choose. Jackets are expected and trainers are not welcome. The upstairs bar takes walk-ins when the dining room is full.
places.tickets: A la carte. Oysters 5.75 pounds each, soup 11.95 pounds, mains considerably more. Reservations strongly recommended and taken online.
places.getting_there: Covent Garden or Leicester Square Underground, both about five minutes on foot. Maiden Lane is a side street off Southampton Street.
places.location_context: Maiden Lane in Covent Garden, a quiet lane one street back from the Strand, minutes from the opera house and the theatres.
places.time_needed: Two hours for dinner.
places.verdict: Come for the game between August and January and book ahead. Outside that season it is a beautiful room charging a premium for competent traditional cooking.

places.name: St John
places.headline: Bring Your Own Wine for Thirty-Two Pounds Corkage
places.body:
St John serves lunch Monday to Sunday from 12.00pm to 3pm, a bar menu from 3pm to 5pm, and supper from 5.30pm, and it charges 32 pounds corkage for a bottle you bring yourself, 42 for sparkling or dessert wine and 84 for a magnum of champagne.

The restaurant opened in 1994 and effectively invented what the world now calls modern British cooking: bone marrow and parsley salad, offal treated as a first-class ingredient, and a whiteboard menu rewritten twice a day. Everything is spare, whitewashed and deliberately unglamorous.

The menus do not go online until 11.00am for lunch and 5.00pm for supper, because they are written that morning. That is not a marketing conceit, it is the reason the food is good.
places.what_great: A restaurant that changed British cooking and still cooks the same way. Roast bone marrow and parsley salad, which is the single most influential plate of food in modern Britain. Corkage, which almost nowhere at this level offers.
places.what_ruined: The room is bright, white and loud, which people either love or find punishing. The menu is genuinely offal-heavy and does not apologise. Smithfield is dead quiet at night, so the walk to and from it is bleak.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a restaurant that is both historically important and still excellent. Five for safety. Four for value: not cheap, but corkage and honest portions make it far better value than its reputation suggests.
places.meta_description: St John in London serves lunch 12 to 3 and supper from 5.30pm, and charges 32 pounds corkage. The restaurant that invented modern British cooking.

places.what_it_is: A restaurant near Smithfield market, open since 1994, serving whole-animal British cooking from a menu rewritten twice a day in a converted smokehouse.
places.why_go: Because this is where modern British food started, and because it is one of the very few genuinely influential restaurants that has not drifted into being a museum of itself.
places.the_good: Bone marrow and parsley salad. A menu rewritten twice daily. Corkage at 32 pounds. Bread and eccles cakes good enough that people come only for those.
places.the_downsides: A hard, bright, loud room. Heavily offal-focused. Smithfield at night is deserted. Booking is needed well ahead for supper.
places.best_for: Anyone curious about British cooking beyond the clichés, and anyone with a good bottle at home worth the corkage.
places.skip_if: Offal is a hard no for you. The menu can be navigated around it, but you would be ordering the least interesting third of it.
places.practical: Check the menu online after 11.00am for lunch or 5.00pm for supper, because it is not written before then. Bring a bottle: 32 pounds corkage on a good wine beats almost any list in London. The bar takes walk-ins.
places.tickets: A la carte, with prices in the mid range for central London. Corkage 32 pounds a bottle, 42 for sparkling or dessert wine, 64 for magnums of wine, 84 for magnums of champagne. Book ahead for supper.
places.getting_there: Farringdon station, five minutes on foot. St John Street runs north from Smithfield market.
places.location_context: Smithfield, on the edge of the City, beside the old meat market. Busy by day with market and office trade, and very quiet after dark.
places.time_needed: Two hours.
places.verdict: Bring a bottle, check the menu after 11am, and order the bone marrow. The most important restaurant in Britain and still one of the best.

places.name: St Paul's Cathedral
places.headline: Twenty-Seven Pounds, and the Dome Climb Is the Part You Will Remember
places.body:
St Paul's charges 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 per child for Monday to Saturday sightseeing, with discounts for families and groups. Sunday is a day of worship rather than sightseeing, which catches a lot of visitors out.

The cathedral floor is impressive and the crypt holds Nelson and Wellington, but the thing that makes the ticket worth it is the climb. The Whispering Gallery, then the Stone Gallery, then the Golden Gallery, each higher and each with a better view, ending on an external walkway around the dome with London laid out underneath.

If you cannot or would rather not climb several hundred steps, you are paying full price for perhaps half the experience, and that is worth knowing before you book.
places.what_great: The dome galleries give one of the best views in London and the climb is a genuine experience rather than a lift ride. Wren's interior is magnificent on its own terms, and the crypt is a serious historical stop. Child admission at 10.50 pounds is reasonable, with family and group discounts available.
places.what_ruined: Twenty-seven pounds is steep, and the best part of it is a 528-step climb that excludes a lot of visitors. Sightseeing is Monday to Saturday only, so a Sunday arrival cannot do the paid visit at all. The upper galleries are narrow and can feel uncomfortable when busy.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the dome and the galleries are genuinely memorable and the interior is magnificent. Value is three because 27 pounds is a lot and the best part of it requires 528 steps you may not want to climb.
places.meta_description: St Paul's costs 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 per child for Monday to Saturday sightseeing. Why the dome climb is the part that justifies the ticket.

places.what_it_is: Christopher Wren's cathedral on Ludgate Hill, completed in 1711 after the Great Fire, with a dome that dominated the London skyline for two and a half centuries and three climbable galleries inside and around it.
places.why_go: For the dome climb and the view from the Golden Gallery, and for one of the finest church interiors in Britain. The Whispering Gallery is a genuine acoustic curiosity rather than a marketing line.
places.the_good: The climb is memorable in a way lift-served viewpoints never are, and each of the three galleries is a distinct experience. The crypt holds Nelson, Wellington and Wren himself. The building sits at the foot of the Millennium Bridge, so it combines naturally with Tate Modern across the river.
places.the_downsides: At 27 pounds it is expensive, and the climb that justifies the price is inaccessible to many. Sightseeing does not run on Sundays. The upper stairs are narrow, enclosed and slow when the cathedral is busy, which makes them hard work on a warm day.
places.best_for: Anyone who can manage several hundred steps and wants the best earned view in London, plus visitors interested in Wren, in English naval and military history, or in church architecture.
places.skip_if: You cannot climb stairs comfortably, in which case a large part of the ticket value is unavailable to you. Skip it also if you have already committed to Westminster Abbey and are watching the budget.
places.practical: Go early on a weekday and climb first while your legs are fresh and the stairwells are quiet. Check that your visit is not on a Sunday. Cross the Millennium Bridge to Tate Modern afterwards, which costs nothing and is the best short walk in the city.
places.tickets: Monday to Saturday sightseeing is 27 pounds per adult and 10.50 pounds per child, with discounts for families and groups. Sunday is a day of worship and sightseeing admission does not operate.
places.getting_there: St Paul's on the Central line is directly outside. Mansion House and Blackfriars are both short walks, and the Millennium Bridge connects on foot to Bankside and Tate Modern.
places.location_context: Ludgate Hill in the City of London, the financial district, which means the surrounding streets are busy on weekdays and notably quiet at weekends. The riverside and Bankside are a five-minute walk over the bridge.
places.time_needed: Two hours including the full climb. Around an hour if you stay on the cathedral floor and in the crypt.
places.accessibility: The cathedral floor and crypt are accessible, but the Whispering, Stone and Golden Galleries are reached only by stairs, so the dome section of the visit is not available to everyone.
places.verdict: Worth the money if you are going to climb it, and questionable value if you are not. Book a weekday morning, go up before you look around at ground level, and pair it with the free walk over the Millennium Bridge to Tate Modern.

places.name: Tate Modern
places.headline: Free Entry to a Power Station Full of Modern Art, and the View Is Free Too
places.body:
Tate Modern occupies the former Bankside Power Station, and the building is the reason to go even if the art leaves you cold. Admission to the permanent collection is free, with opening from 10.00 Sunday to Thursday.

The Turbine Hall is the space everyone photographs, a vast former machine room now used for single large commissions. It is free, it takes ten minutes, and it is one of the few genuinely surprising interior spaces in London.

The upper levels give wide views across the Thames to St Paul's, and they also cost nothing. On a clear afternoon that view is competitive with paid viewing platforms elsewhere in the city.
places.what_great: Free admission to the permanent collection, free views over the river, and a building that would be worth visiting empty. Under-11s go free with a parent, 16 to 25-year-olds can join Tate Collective for cheap exhibition tickets, and companions of disabled visitors go free.
places.what_ruined: The permanent collection is uneven and the labelling is often more confident than the work. Paid exhibitions sit inside a free museum. Weekends in the Turbine Hall are extremely crowded, and the layout across two linked buildings confuses almost everyone on a first visit.
places.rating_rationale: Four because modern art divides people and this collection will not convert a sceptic. Value is five without qualification: the permanent collection and the river views cost nothing.
places.meta_description: Tate Modern is free, open Sunday to Thursday from 10.00, and the upper-floor views over the Thames cost nothing at all.

places.what_it_is: A national gallery of international modern and contemporary art on the south bank of the Thames, housed in the converted Bankside Power Station, with the Turbine Hall as its central space.
places.why_go: For the building, for the free river views from the upper floors, and for a collection that covers the twentieth century broadly. The Turbine Hall commissions are frequently the most talked-about art installations in the country.
places.the_good: It is free, it is open late enough on most days to be an evening stop, and the views cost nothing. The Tate Collective scheme gives 16 to 25-year-olds cheap exhibition access. It sits directly on the river walk, so it combines with the Millennium Bridge and St Paul's without any transport.
places.the_downsides: The permanent hang is uneven, and visitors who do not already like modern art rarely leave converted. Special exhibitions are paid, which surprises people in a free museum. The two-building layout is genuinely confusing and the crowding at weekends is severe.
places.best_for: Anyone already interested in modern art, visitors on a budget, people who like industrial architecture, and anyone wanting a free high view over central London.
places.skip_if: Modern and contemporary art actively annoys you. Nothing here will change that, and the National Gallery on the other side of the river is free too and holds work you may prefer.
places.practical: Go on a weekday, enter through the Turbine Hall ramp for the full effect of the space, and go up to the upper levels for the view before you look at any art. Combine it with the Millennium Bridge crossing to St Paul's, which takes five minutes and is the best short walk in central London.
places.tickets: The permanent collection is free. Exhibitions are ticketed, with members getting unlimited free entry. Up to four children aged 11 and under go free per parent or guardian, visitors aged 16 to 25 can join Tate Collective for 5 pound exhibition tickets, and entry for companions of disabled visitors is free.
places.getting_there: Southwark on the Jubilee line and Blackfriars on the Circle and District lines are both short walks. From St Paul's on the Central line, cross the Millennium Bridge on foot.
places.location_context: Bankside, on the south bank of the Thames facing St Paul's Cathedral, on the stretch of riverside walk that runs from the Globe to Borough Market. The immediate area is well served for food and busy in the evenings.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the collection and the views. The Turbine Hall alone is a worthwhile fifteen-minute stop if you are passing.
places.accessibility: Entry for companions of disabled visitors is free. The building is served by lifts throughout and the main Turbine Hall entrance is a long step-free ramp.
places.verdict: Worth going for the building and the view even if the art is not your thing, and unbeatable value because both are free. Go on a weekday, take the river view first, and cross the Millennium Bridge afterwards.

places.name: Westminster Abbey
places.headline: Thirty-One Pounds to Walk Through a Thousand Years of English History
places.body:
Westminster Abbey charges 31 pounds for adult sightseeing admission, with over-65s and students at 28 pounds, children aged 6 to 17 at 14 pounds and under-6s free.

That is a lot of money for a church, and the abbey knows it. What you get for it is the coronation church of the English and British monarchy, the burial place of monarchs, and Poets' Corner, which is a denser concentration of literary graves and memorials than anywhere else in the world.

The honest caveat is that the visit is heavily routed. You follow a set path through a crowded building, and the pace is set by the people in front of you. It rewards knowing in advance which three or four things you want to stand in front of.
places.what_great: The building holds a genuinely unmatched concentration of English history, and Poets' Corner alone justifies a long look. Children aged 6 to 17 pay 14 pounds and under-6s are free, and attending a service costs nothing at all, which is the route most people never consider.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-one pounds is a steep admission and the route through is crowded and one-directional, so lingering is difficult. Photography restrictions apply in much of the building. Prices also vary by date, so the figure you are quoted depends on when you go.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building and what is inside it are extraordinary. Value is three: 31 pounds is among the steepest church admissions in Europe and the visit is tightly routed.
places.meta_description: Westminster Abbey costs 31 pounds for adults, 28 for over-65s and students, and 14 for children. What the ticket includes and when it is worth it.

places.what_it_is: A royal church in Westminster, the coronation site of English and British monarchs since 1066, the burial place of many of them, and home to Poets' Corner. It is a working church as well as a visitor attraction.
places.why_go: Because no other single building holds this much of English history in one place. The coronation chair, the royal tombs and Poets' Corner are all inside one route.
places.the_good: The concentration of history is genuinely without equal, the audio guide is included rather than an extra, and there are real child and concession rates. Attending a service is free, which is by far the cheapest way to be inside the building.
places.the_downsides: At 31 pounds it is among the most expensive church admissions in Europe. The visitor route is one-way and crowded, so you move at the speed of the group. Prices shift by date, so the published rate depends on when you look. Photography is restricted through much of the interior.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in English history or literature, first-time visitors to London who want one major historic interior, and families who benefit from the 14 pound child rate.
places.skip_if: You are on a budget and have already paid for St Paul's. Two expensive church visits in one trip is a lot, and St Paul's dome climb is the more physically memorable of the two. Also skip the paid visit if you would be content attending a service instead.
places.practical: Book online for a specific time and go early, because the route congests badly by late morning. If cost is the obstacle, check service times and attend one, which is free and puts you inside the same building. Allow more time than you think for Poets' Corner, which is where the visit is actually worth the money.
places.tickets: Published sightseeing prices are 31 pounds for adults and families of one adult and one child, 28 pounds for over-65s and students, 14 pounds for children aged 6 to 17, and free for children aged 0 to 5 and Association members. Prices are published in dated bands, so the exact figure varies with the period of your visit.
places.getting_there: Westminster on the Circle, District and Jubilee lines is a two-minute walk. St James's Park on the Circle and District lines is a similar distance from the other side.
places.location_context: Westminster, directly beside the Houses of Parliament and across from Parliament Square. The area is dense with government buildings and heavy with tour groups, and it is a short walk along the river to the London Eye.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the full route with the audio guide. Less if you are moving briskly, but the routing makes it hard to go much faster than the crowd allows.
places.verdict: Extraordinary building, uncomfortable price. Worth it once if English history or literature matters to you, and best experienced early in the day before the route jams. If money is tight, go to a service instead and see the same interior for nothing.
places.accessibility: Step-free access throughout the main route, with hearing loops and audio guides. Mobility aids including manual wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge, and a lift gives step-free wheelchair access to the galleries. The cloisters are the exception, reached by ten steps and a steep ramp. The nearest step-free Underground station is Westminster.

places.name: Museo Frida Kahlo
places.headline: Three Hundred and Twenty Pesos, and You Cannot Buy It at the Door
places.body:
The Museo Frida Kahlo charges 320 pesos for general admission, 160 pesos for Mexican residents with official identification, 60 pesos for students and teachers with a valid card, and 30 pesos for seniors and children aged 6 to 12. There is no ticket office: everything is bought online.

The Casa Azul is the house Kahlo was born in, lived in with Diego Rivera, and died in, and it is kept as a house rather than converted into a gallery. The kitchen, the studio, the wheelchair at the easel and the bed with the mirror above it do more than any wall text.

It is closed on Mondays, opens at 11:00 on Wednesdays and at 10:00 on other days, and it is small, so the timed slots sell out well ahead.
places.what_great: The house itself, preserved rather than staged. The studio and the bedroom, which are genuinely affecting. The garden, which is a rare quiet space in Coyoacan.
places.what_ruined: Three hundred and twenty pesos is the highest museum price in Mexico City and roughly double what residents pay. No tickets at the door means an unplanned visit is impossible. The rooms are small and the timed slots still feel crowded.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a house museum that could not be replaced. Five for safety in Coyoacan. Three for value: 320 pesos for a small house, with residents paying half, is a tourist price and reads as one.
places.meta_description: The Museo Frida Kahlo in Mexico City costs 320 pesos, 160 for residents, and sells no tickets at the door. The Casa Azul, kept as a house.

places.what_it_is: The Casa Azul in Coyoacan, Frida Kahlo's family home, preserved as a house museum with her studio, personal effects, wardrobe and a small selection of her paintings.
places.why_go: Because the house explains the paintings. The mirror above the bed, the corsets and the wheelchair at the easel make the work legible in a way a gallery hang never does.
places.the_good: An intact artist's house, a beautiful garden, the reconstructed studio, and the wardrobe exhibition of her clothing and medical corsets.
places.the_downsides: The most expensive museum ticket in the city, at double the resident rate. Online-only sales. Small rooms that fill instantly. Closed Mondays.
places.best_for: Anyone with any interest in Kahlo, and anyone curious about how Mexico City's intellectual left lived in the 1930s and 1940s.
places.skip_if: You cannot book in advance. Turning up without a ticket means not getting in, not queueing.
places.practical: Book online days ahead and take the earliest slot. Combine it with the Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera and the Coyoacan market, both nearby. Wednesday opening is 11:00, not 10:00.
places.tickets: General admission 320 pesos, Mexican residents with official ID 160 pesos, students and teachers with a valid card 60 pesos, seniors and children aged 6 to 12 30 pesos. Sold online only; there is no ticket office.
places.getting_there: Metro line 3 to Coyoacan then a twenty-minute walk, or a taxi to Londres 247. Most visitors come by app taxi from the centre, about forty minutes.
places.location_context: Coyoacan, a colonial village absorbed by the city, with cobbled streets, a market and plazas, and a very different pace from central Mexico City.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes including the garden.
places.accessibility: The ground floor and garden are largely accessible; the upper studio is reached by stairs only.
places.verdict: Book online days ahead or do not go. Expensive and small, and still one of the best house museums anywhere.

places.name: Museo Nacional de Antropologia
places.headline: Two Hundred and Ten Pesos for the Best Archaeology Museum in the Americas
places.body:
The Museo Nacional de Antropologia charges 210 pesos for general admission and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and foreign residents. It opens Tuesday to Sunday from 9:00 to 18:00.

It is the best museum of its kind anywhere in the Americas and it is not a close contest. The Aztec Sun Stone, the Olmec heads, the reconstructed tomb of Pakal from Palenque and a full-scale replica of the Bonampak murals are all here, arranged by culture around a courtyard with a vast concrete umbrella pouring water from a single column.

The building, by Pedro Ramirez Vazquez and finished in 1964, is as important as anything in it, and the upper floor on living indigenous cultures is the part almost everyone skips and should not.
places.what_great: The Sun Stone, the Olmec heads and Pakal's tomb in one building. The courtyard and its fountain. Two hundred and ten pesos for a collection that would cost three times as much anywhere else.
places.what_ruined: It is too large to see properly in a day and most people try. English labelling is inconsistent. It sits in Chapultepec, so the walk in from the road is longer than expected, and Sunday is free for nationals and correspondingly packed.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a collection with no equal in the hemisphere. Four for safety, with normal Mexico City caution on the approach. Five for value: 210 pesos is roughly ten euros for a full day.
places.meta_description: The Museo Nacional de Antropologia in Mexico City costs 210 pesos, 105 for residents, open Tuesday to Sunday 9:00 to 18:00. The Sun Stone and the Olmec heads.

places.what_it_is: Mexico's national museum of anthropology, in Chapultepec Park, holding the country's pre-Columbian archaeological collections on the ground floor and its living indigenous cultures upstairs.
places.why_go: Because everything you will see at Teotihuacan, Palenque, Monte Alban and Chichen Itza is explained here, and because the Sun Stone in person is not the object the photographs suggest.
places.the_good: An unrivalled collection, a masterpiece of a building, the Bonampak murals, the Pakal tomb reconstruction, and a price that is a fraction of the equivalent elsewhere.
places.the_downsides: Far too big for one visit. Patchy English labelling. Crowded on Sundays when nationals enter free. The upper floor is quiet because most people run out of stamina.
places.best_for: Every visitor to Mexico City, and essential before any trip to the archaeological sites.
places.skip_if: Nothing, really. If time is short, do the Mexica and Maya halls and leave the rest.
places.practical: Go on a weekday morning. Do the Mexica hall with the Sun Stone first, then Maya, then Teotihuacan, and accept that you will not see it all. Avoid Sunday unless crowds do not bother you.
places.tickets: General admission 210.00 pesos; Mexican nationals and foreign residents 105.00 pesos. Sunday is free for Mexican nationals and residents. Parking is 50.00 pesos per hour.
places.getting_there: Metro line 7 to Auditorio, then a ten-minute walk through the park, or line 1 to Chapultepec and a longer walk. Buses along Reforma stop outside.
places.location_context: Chapultepec Park, the large forested park west of the centre, alongside the Rufino Tamayo museum and the Museo de Arte Moderno, with Chapultepec Castle on the hill nearby.
places.time_needed: Half a day minimum, a full day if you intend to see the upper floor.
places.accessibility: Step-free with ramps and lifts throughout both floors, and wheelchairs available to borrow.
places.verdict: The best museum in Mexico and one of the best anywhere. Two hundred and ten pesos, a weekday morning, and start with the Sun Stone.

places.name: Duomo di Milano
places.headline: Twenty-Two Euros to Walk on the Roof of the Cathedral
places.body:
The Duomo sells tickets by what you want to see. The complete visit, covering the cathedral interior, the terraces and the museum, starts from 22 euros full price and 11 euros reduced. A cathedral and museum ticket without the terraces starts from 8 euros full and 4 reduced, and the terraces alone start from 16 euros full and 8 reduced.

The terraces are the reason to pay the full price. You walk on the roof, among the flying buttresses and the 135 spires, close enough to see the carving on statues that were never meant to be looked at from below. There is no other cathedral in Europe where you can do this.

The interior is vast and dim and worth an hour, but the roof is what people remember for the rest of their lives.
places.what_great: Walking on the roof among the spires, which nowhere else offers. A reduced price of 11 euros for the complete visit. The stained glass in the apse, which is the best in Italy.
places.what_ruined: The ticket structure is genuinely confusing and there are at least five combinations. The queue for the terraces at midday in summer is brutal. Bare shoulders and knees are refused at the door and people arrive dressed for a hot day.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the roof terraces, which are unique. Four for safety, only for pickpockets working the queue on the piazza. Four for value: 22 euros is fair but the tiered pricing invites mistakes.
places.meta_description: The Duomo di Milano costs from 22 euros for the complete visit with terraces, 8 euros without. Walking on the cathedral roof among the spires.

places.what_it_is: Milan's gothic cathedral, begun in 1386 and finished over six centuries, with an interior, a museum, an archaeological area and roof terraces open to visitors.
places.why_go: The terraces. Walking among the spires and buttresses of a gothic cathedral roof is something almost no other building in Europe permits, and it changes how you see the front of it from the square.
places.the_good: The roof walk, the apse windows, the sheer scale of the interior, and a museum that explains six centuries of construction.
places.the_downsides: A confusing menu of ticket types. Long midday queues. A strict dress code enforced at the door. The lift to the terraces costs more than the stairs.
places.best_for: Every visitor to Milan. If you buy one ticket in the city, buy this one.
places.skip_if: You are afraid of heights or cannot manage stairs, in which case buy the cathedral and museum ticket and skip the terraces.
places.practical: Buy the complete visit online and go to the terraces first thing or in the last two hours. Cover shoulders and knees or you will be turned away. Take the stairs if you are able: the queue is shorter than for the lift.
places.tickets: Complete visit with terraces from 22 euros full, 11 reduced. Cathedral and museum from 8 euros full, 4 reduced. Terraces alone from 16 euros full, 8 reduced.
places.getting_there: Metro lines 1 and 3 to Duomo, which surfaces directly onto the piazza.
places.location_context: Piazza del Duomo, the exact centre of Milan, with the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II on one side and the shopping streets radiating out from it.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the complete visit, more if the queues are long.
places.accessibility: The cathedral and museum are step-free; the terraces are reachable by lift, though the roof walk itself is uneven and has steps.
places.verdict: Buy the complete visit, go up first, and cover your shoulders. The roof of the Duomo is the best twenty-two euros in Milan.

places.name: Pinacoteca di Brera
places.headline: Twenty Euros, and Four If You Are Between Eighteen and Twenty-Five
places.body:
The Pinacoteca di Brera charges 20.00 euros for a full Grande Brera ticket and 4.00 euros reduced for visitors aged 18 to 25. Audioguides are 5.00 euros and radioguides 2.00 euros.

The collection is northern Italian painting at its peak: Piero della Francesca's Brera Madonna, Mantegna's Dead Christ seen from the soles of the feet, Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus, Bellini, Tintoretto, Veronese. Any one of them would anchor a museum.

It shares a seventeenth-century palazzo with the art academy, so the courtyard is full of students, and the recently opened Palazzo Citterio next door extends the ticket into the twentieth century.
places.what_great: The Mantegna and the Piero della Francesca in adjacent rooms. Four euros for anyone aged 18 to 25, which is close to a gift. Far quieter than the Duomo two streets away.
places.what_ruined: Twenty euros is at the top of the Italian range for a picture gallery. The hang assumes you know your Renaissance schools. The Brera district around it is expensive enough that lunch afterwards costs as much as the ticket.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a collection of this quality. Five for safety in Brera. Four for value: fair at twenty euros, exceptional at four for the under-26s.

places.why_go: For Mantegna's Dead Christ and Piero della Francesca's Brera Madonna, two of the most radical paintings of the Italian Renaissance, hanging within a few metres of each other.
places.the_good: An outstanding collection with genuine masterpieces rather than school pieces, a four euro ticket for 18 to 25 year olds, and far fewer people than the cathedral.
places.the_downsides: Expensive at full price. Little help for a visitor who does not already know the period. Audioguides cost extra.

places.time_needed: Two hours, three with Palazzo Citterio.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve the gallery floors and the route through the collection is step-free.
places.verdict: Go for the Mantegna. Twenty euros is fair, four euros for the under-26s is a bargain, and it is the quietest great gallery in Italy.

places.name: Alte Pinakothek
places.headline: Nine Euros Most Days and One Euro on Sunday, Which Is Almost Absurd
places.body:
The Alte Pinakothek charges 9 euro regular admission and 6 euro reduced, and on Sundays it is 1 euro. Admission is free for children and young people under the age of 18.

The Sunday rate is not a promotion. It is a standing Bavarian policy across the state collections, and it means one of the world's great holdings of European painting from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century costs about the same as a coffee.

The collection's strengths are Old German and Early Netherlandish painting, Rubens at a depth found nowhere else, and Italian work from the Renaissance. It is the sort of museum where the second-rank rooms in most galleries would be the highlight.
places.what_great: Nine euro regular admission is remarkable for a collection of this standing, and the 1 euro Sunday rate is close to absurd. Under-18s go free. The Rubens holdings in particular are unmatched, and the building is calm and well lit for looking at paintings.
places.what_ruined: The 1 euro Sunday is well known locally, so Sundays are correspondingly busy. Closed Mondays, which catches visitors out. The building sits in a museum quarter rather than a lively part of the city, so there is little around it.
places.rating_rationale: Five throughout. The collection is one of the most important holdings of old master painting in the world, regular admission is 9 euro, and on Sundays it is 1 euro.
places.meta_description: The Alte Pinakothek costs 9 euro regular, 6 reduced, and 1 euro on Sundays. Under-18s free. One of Europe's great collections.

places.why_go: For the Rubens rooms, which have no equal anywhere, and for Old German and Early Netherlandish painting shown at a depth that most national galleries cannot approach.
places.the_good: Nine euro regular admission, 6 euro reduced and 1 euro on Sundays, with under-18s free. A first-rank collection in a calm, well-lit building. It sits alongside the Neue Pinakothek and Pinakothek der Moderne, so a museum day needs no travel.
places.the_downsides: Sundays are busy precisely because of the 1 euro rate. Closed on Mondays. The Kunstareal is a quiet institutional district with little atmosphere, so there is not much reason to linger outside the museums.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in old master painting, budget travellers given the Sunday rate, and families since under-18s go free.

places.practical: Go on a Sunday for the 1 euro rate but arrive at opening, since everyone else in Munich knows about it too. Avoid Mondays entirely. Combine with the Neue Pinakothek or Pinakothek der Moderne, which are a two-minute walk away.

places.time_needed: Two to three hours. The Rubens rooms alone can take an hour if you let them.
places.accessibility: The museum is served by lifts and publishes accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: One of the best-value great museums in Europe, and on Sundays it is almost free. Go early on a Sunday, never on a Monday, and give the Rubens rooms more time than you planned.

places.name: Deutsches Museum
places.headline: Sixteen Euros for the Largest Science Museum in the World
places.body:
The Deutsches Museum on the Museumsinsel charges 16 euros for a day ticket for adults aged 18 and over, 9 euros discounted with valid ID, and 33 euros for a family ticket covering up to two adults with their own children aged 17 and under.

It is, by the usual measures, the largest museum of science and technology in the world, and the collection runs from mining galleries in the basement to aircraft hanging from the ceiling. The mining exhibition is a full reconstructed pit you walk through underground, which is the part children remember for years.

A long renovation has reopened in phases, so the museum you visit now is not the one in older guidebooks. Check what is open before you go, because whole departments have moved or are still behind hoardings.
places.what_great: Genuine scale, with real aircraft, real ships and a walk-through mine rather than screens about them. Sixteen euros is remarkable value for the size of it. The family ticket at 33 euros makes a day out affordable.
places.what_ruined: It is too big to see in a day and the phased renovation means sections close without much warning. Signage in English is inconsistent in the older halls, and the sheer volume of exhibits with limited interpretation can be numbing.
places.rating_rationale: Five across the board. It is the biggest museum of its kind on earth, it is entirely safe, and sixteen euros for a full day inside it is among the best value in western Europe.
places.meta_description: The Deutsches Museum in Munich costs 16 euros for adults, 9 discounted and 33 for a family. The largest science and technology museum in the world.

places.what_it_is: The world's largest museum of science and technology, on an island in the Isar in central Munich, covering mining, aviation, shipping, physics, chemistry and astronomy across many halls.
places.why_go: For scale and for real objects. This is a museum of actual submarines, aircraft and machinery rather than a science centre of interactive panels, and there is nothing else quite this size.
places.the_good: Enormous, cheap for what it is, and strong on genuine artefacts. The reconstructed mine is a highlight. Family ticket pricing is generous.
places.the_downsides: Impossible to finish in one visit. The renovation has been running for years and closes sections in phases. English interpretation is patchy in the older galleries.
places.best_for: Families, anyone technically minded, and rainy days, of which Munich has plenty.
places.skip_if: You have half a day. This needs a proper commitment or it becomes a route march past things you do not have time to read about.
places.practical: Check which departments are open before you go. Start with the mine, which gets busy, then pick two or three other halls rather than trying to walk everything. A one-euro coin is needed as a deposit for the lockers.
places.tickets: Adult day ticket 16 euros, discounted 9 euros with valid ID, family ticket 33 euros for up to two adults with their own children aged 17 and under. An annual pass covering all three Munich sites is 50 euros, 25 reduced.
places.getting_there: S-Bahn to Isartor then a five-minute walk across the bridge, or tram 16 to Deutsches Museum. It is a fifteen-minute walk from Marienplatz.
places.location_context: Museumsinsel, an island in the Isar just south of the old centre, with the river on both sides and a pleasant walk north along the bank into the Altstadt.
places.time_needed: Half a day minimum. A full day is easy, and regulars come back repeatedly.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve the main exhibition levels and level 1 can be reached by stairs or lift; some historic halls remain harder to navigate.
places.verdict: Sixteen euros for the largest science museum on earth is the best value in Munich. Check what is open, pick three halls, and do not try to see it all.

places.name: Hofbrauhaus
places.headline: Open Every Day From Eleven Until Midnight, and Everyone Knows It
places.body:
The Hofbrauhaus opens every day from 11.00 to 0.00, with the kitchen closing at 22.00 and last serving at 23.30. There is no reservation for the main hall and no closed day in the year.

It is the most famous beer hall in the world, founded as the ducal brewery in 1589, and on any given evening the ground floor holds around a thousand people, a brass band, and a queue at the door. Regulars have lockers for their personal steins along one wall, which tells you the place is not purely a tourist exhibit, though it is substantially one.

The food is Bavarian and competent rather than good. The beer, served in litre Mass, is the reason to be there, along with the noise, which is considerable.
places.what_great: Open every single day until midnight, which in Munich matters more than it sounds. Litre steins, a live band, and a genuine 400-year-old institution. Free to walk in and look even if you do not sit down.
places.what_ruined: The food is the weakest part and priced as though it were not. It is overwhelmingly tourists, and the staff process them accordingly. Loud to the point where conversation is work, and finding a table on a summer evening can take half an hour.
places.rating_rationale: Three because it is an institution worth seeing that is no longer a good restaurant. Four for safety, with the usual caution around very drunk crowds late on. Three for value: the beer is fairly priced, the food is not.
places.meta_description: The Hofbrauhaus in Munich opens daily 11.00 to midnight, kitchen closes 22.00. Go for the beer hall and the band, not for the food.

places.what_it_is: Munich's state-owned beer hall on the Platzl, founded as the ducal brewery in 1589, with a thousand-seat ground floor hall, a brass band and Bavarian food.
places.why_go: To stand inside the building every other beer hall in the world is imitating, and to drink a Mass while a band plays. It is a spectacle, and it is honest about being one.
places.the_good: Daily opening until midnight, litre steins, the band, the sheer scale of the room, and the regulars' stein lockers on the wall.
places.the_downsides: Mediocre, overpriced food. Overwhelmingly tourist trade. Extremely loud. Long waits for a table in summer.
places.best_for: First-time visitors to Munich, and groups, who suit the long shared tables far better than couples do.
places.skip_if: You want a good Bavarian meal. Augustiner-Keller and the Viktualienmarkt beer garden both do the food better with a fraction of the crowd.
places.practical: Go for a late morning or mid-afternoon beer when the hall is calm enough to look at. Eat elsewhere. Shared tables are the norm, so ask before sitting down at one.
places.tickets: No reservation for the main hall; walk in and find a table. Upper floors take group bookings. Beer is sold by the Mass, a full litre.
places.getting_there: S-Bahn or U-Bahn to Marienplatz, then a three-minute walk east to the Platzl.
places.location_context: The Platzl, a small square in the old town two minutes from Marienplatz, surrounded by souvenir shops and the Hotel Platzl.
places.time_needed: An hour for a beer, two if you eat.
places.verdict: Worth one beer for the room and the band. Eat somewhere else, and go in the afternoon when you can actually see the place.

places.name: Pinakothek der Moderne
places.headline: Ten Euros, One Euro on Sunday, and Four Museums Under One Roof
places.body:
The Pinakothek der Moderne charges 10 euro admission with 7 euro reduced, and 1 euro on Sundays. Children and young people under 18 receive free admission.

The Sunday rate is standing Bavarian policy across the state collections rather than a promotion, and it applies here exactly as it does at the Alte Pinakothek across the square.

What makes this building unusual is that it houses four separate institutions: the modern art collection, the Neue Sammlung design museum, the architecture museum of the Technical University, and the state collection of works on paper. The design museum in the basement is the one most visitors underestimate and the one most of them end up talking about afterwards, because it covers everything from Bauhaus furniture to industrial design and a genuinely serious car collection.
places.what_great: Ten euro for four museums, dropping to 1 euro on Sundays, with under-18s free. The Neue Sammlung design collection is world class and consistently surprises people who came for the paintings. The Stephan Braunfels rotunda is a fine piece of museum architecture in its own right.
places.what_ruined: Four institutions under one roof means uneven signage and visitors missing whole sections, particularly the basement design museum. Closed Mondays. Sundays are busy for the obvious reason. The Kunstareal district around it is institutional and quiet, with little to do outside the museums.
places.rating_rationale: Four because combining four collections in one building is a strength and a scheduling problem in equal measure. Value is five: 10 euro standard, 1 euro on Sundays, free under 18.
places.meta_description: The Pinakothek der Moderne costs 10 euro, 7 reduced, and 1 euro on Sundays, with under-18s free. Art, design, architecture and works on paper.

places.why_go: For the Neue Sammlung, which is one of the strongest design collections anywhere and covers furniture, industrial design and vehicles, and for twentieth-century art shown alongside it rather than in isolation.
places.the_good: Four museums for one 10 euro ticket, 1 euro on Sundays, free for under-18s. The design collection is exceptional and underrated. It sits two minutes from the Alte Pinakothek, so a full museum day needs no travel.
places.the_downsides: The four-in-one arrangement confuses people and the basement design museum is regularly missed entirely. Closed on Mondays. Sunday is cheap and correspondingly crowded. The surrounding district has little life outside museum hours.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in design or architecture as much as painting, budget travellers who can time a Sunday, and families given free under-18 entry.
places.skip_if: You have one museum slot in Munich and prefer old masters, in which case the Alte Pinakothek across the square is the better ticket. Do not arrive on a Monday.
places.practical: Go on a Sunday for the 1 euro rate but arrive at opening. Start in the basement with the Neue Sammlung, because that is the section people run out of time for. Combine with the Alte Pinakothek, two minutes away, for a full day.
places.tickets: Admission is 10 euro with 7 euro reduced, and 1 euro on Sundays. Children and young people under 18 receive free admission. Tickets can be bought in advance through the museum webshop.
places.getting_there: U2 to Theresienstrasse or Konigsplatz, or tram 27 to Pinakotheken. About twenty minutes on foot from Munich Hauptbahnhof.
places.location_context: The Kunstareal in Maxvorstadt, sharing the district with the Alte Pinakothek, the Neue Pinakothek, the Brandhorst and the Glyptothek. Quiet, green and entirely institutional.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours to do all four collections properly. Ninety minutes if you pick two.
places.accessibility: The building is served by lifts throughout and the collections publish accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: The best-value modern museum in Munich, especially on a Sunday. Go for the design collection in the basement rather than only the paintings, and pair it with the Alte Pinakothek across the square.

places.name: National WWII Museum
places.headline: Twenty-Seven Dollars to Start, and the Packages Climb From There
places.body:
The National WWII Museum sells general admission starting at $27, an Essentials package starting at $36 that adds the Beyond All Boundaries 4D cinematic experience, and a Best Value package starting at $39 that adds the Freedom Theater experience as well.

It is the official museum of the Second World War in the United States and it occupies several buildings across a campus in the Warehouse District. The aircraft hanging in the Boeing Center, the D-Day exhibition and the Road to Berlin and Road to Tokyo galleries are all substantial, and the whole thing takes far longer than people plan for.

The presentation is unashamedly emotional, with personal dog tags issued at the entrance that follow one service member's story through the galleries. It works, and it is worth knowing in advance that it is designed to.
places.what_great: Enormous scope for twenty-seven dollars, real aircraft and vehicles rather than models, and a dog tag device that turns a survey into one person's war. The campus is genuinely well organised.
places.what_ruined: The upsell is relentless: three package tiers, extra experiences and a submarine simulator, all priced separately. It needs a full day and most visitors give it three hours. The tone is celebratory in a way that flattens some of the harder history.
places.rating_rationale: Five for scale and execution. Five for safety in the Warehouse District. Four for value: twenty-seven dollars is fair, but the real cost is whichever package you end up buying.
places.meta_description: The National WWII Museum in New Orleans starts at $27 general admission, $36 with the 4D film. Several buildings, real aircraft, and a full day of it.

places.what_it_is: The United States' official museum of the Second World War, on a multi-building campus in the New Orleans Warehouse District, covering the American war in Europe and the Pacific.
places.why_go: For the scale and for the objects. Aircraft, landing craft and vehicles in the room with you, plus the best D-Day exhibition anywhere, given that the landing craft themselves were built in New Orleans.
places.the_good: Several substantial buildings, genuine aircraft and vehicles, a strong D-Day gallery, and a personal dog tag that gives the visit a thread.
places.the_downsides: Aggressive package upselling. Needs a full day. A celebratory register that avoids some of the harder questions. Popular enough that midday is crowded.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in the Second World War, and families with teenagers.
places.skip_if: You have half a day in New Orleans. The French Quarter and the Garden District are the better use of it.
places.practical: Arrive at opening and plan a full day. Decide on the package before you get to the counter, because deciding at the desk is how people spend forty dollars they did not intend to. The 4D film is worth it once.

places.getting_there: The St Charles or Riverfront streetcar to the Warehouse District, or a fifteen-minute walk from the French Quarter along Magazine Street.
places.location_context: The Warehouse District, south-west of the French Quarter, an area of converted warehouses, galleries and restaurants that is quieter than the Quarter and easy to walk.
places.time_needed: A full day. Four hours is the absolute minimum.
places.accessibility: Fully step-free with lifts between all buildings and levels, and wheelchairs available to borrow.
places.verdict: Give it a whole day, pick your package before you reach the desk, and start at opening. Twenty-seven dollars buys more museum than almost anywhere in the country.

places.name: New Orleans Museum of Art
places.headline: Eighteen Dollars if You Live Here, Twenty-Three if You Do Not, Free Under Twenty
places.body:
The New Orleans Museum of Art charges adults $18 for Louisiana residents and $23 for out-of-state visitors, with seniors aged 65 and up at $13 and $18 and university students with ID at $11 and $16. Youth aged 19 and under enter free regardless of where they live.

The collection is stronger than a city this size has any right to expect: French painting, a serious photography holding, Japanese and African art, and a decorative arts collection built on New Orleans money from the cotton and shipping years.

The Besthoff Sculpture Garden beside it is free, covers eleven acres of live oaks and lagoons in City Park, and is one of the best public spaces in the American South.
places.what_great: Free for everyone aged 19 and under. The Besthoff Sculpture Garden, free and genuinely beautiful. A collection with real depth in photography and French painting.
places.what_ruined: Out-of-state visitors pay five dollars more than residents for the same museum. City Park is a long way from the Quarter and the streetcar takes its time. The building is grand but the galleries are conventional.
places.rating_rationale: Four for a good regional museum that is not a great one. Four for safety: City Park is fine in daylight, less so after dark. Five for value, given free entry under 20 and a free sculpture garden.

places.the_good: Free under 20. A free eleven-acre sculpture garden under live oaks. Strong photography and decorative arts. A calm alternative to the Quarter.
places.the_downsides: Two-tier pricing that charges visitors more. A long trip from the centre. Conventional gallery presentation. Closed on several holidays including Mardi Gras.
places.best_for: Families, given free entry under 20, and anyone wanting a half day away from Bourbon Street.
places.skip_if: You have two days in New Orleans. The WWII Museum and the city itself have the stronger claim.
places.practical: Do the sculpture garden even if you skip the museum, because it is free and open separately. Take the Canal Street streetcar to City Park and allow half an hour each way.

places.getting_there: The Canal Street streetcar to City Park and Museum, which stops at the entrance, about twenty-five minutes from the French Quarter.
places.location_context: City Park, a large park north of the centre with live oaks, lagoons and the sculpture garden, well away from the tourist districts.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the museum, plus an hour for the sculpture garden.
places.accessibility: Step-free with lifts throughout the museum, and the sculpture garden paths are level and paved.
places.verdict: Go for the free sculpture garden and stay for the photography. Free under 20, and the out-of-state surcharge is the only irritating part.

places.name: Empire State Building
places.headline: Forty-Four Dollars Before the Booking Fee, and the Best Reason to Go Is What You Can See
places.body:
Empire State Building tickets start at 44 dollars for the 86th-floor main deck, and a 5 dollar booking charge is added to each transaction, so the real floor is 49 dollars before you have chosen anything.

The counterintuitive argument for coming here rather than a taller, newer observatory is simple: this is the building everyone else is looking at. From One World Observatory or Top of the Rock you get a fine view that happens to contain the Empire State Building. From the Empire State Building you get a view that does not, which matters less than people expect, because what the 86th floor actually offers is an open-air deck in the middle of Midtown at a height where the street grid is still legible.

The 102nd floor is enclosed, higher and costs more. Most people are better served staying at 86.
places.what_great: The 86th-floor deck is open-air, which no enclosed observatory can match: you hear the city as well as see it. Its position mid-island means both downtown and uptown are in view at once. Flexible ticket types allow rescheduling, which is genuinely useful given how much the weather decides here.
places.what_ruined: Tickets start at 44 dollars and a 5 dollar booking charge is added to every transaction, so the advertised price is never the price. The upsell ladder from main deck to 102nd floor to flex tickets is aggressive. Queues at sunset are the worst of the day and that is exactly when everyone wants to be up there.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the 86th-floor deck is an open-air view of a skyline that has no equal. Value is three: tickets start at 44 dollars, a 5 dollar booking charge is added to every transaction, and the upsells climb fast.
places.meta_description: Empire State Building tickets start at 44 dollars plus a 5 dollar booking charge. Which deck to pick, when to go, and why the view beats the taller ones.

places.what_it_is: A 1931 Art Deco skyscraper on Fifth Avenue at 34th Street with two observation decks: the open-air 86th floor and the enclosed 102nd floor near the top of the mast.
places.why_go: For the open-air 86th-floor deck, which sits high enough to see both ends of Manhattan and low enough that the streets below still read as streets rather than as a map. It is the most legible high view in the city.
places.the_good: Open-air rather than behind glass, a central position that shows you more of the island than a downtown observatory does, and rescheduling on the flexible ticket types. The Art Deco lobby and the building's own exhibition are included and are better than they need to be.
places.the_downsides: The starting price is 44 dollars and a 5 dollar booking charge lands on every transaction. The 102nd floor costs meaningfully more for an enclosed view that is not much better. Sunset slots are the most crowded hour of the day, and the deck is genuinely tight when full.
places.best_for: First-time visitors to New York, anyone who wants an open-air view rather than a window, and photographers who can book an off-peak slot.
places.skip_if: You specifically want the Empire State Building in your photograph, in which case Top of the Rock is the better choice. Skip it too if you are doing One World Observatory on the same trip, because two paid high views in one visit is a lot of money for diminishing returns.
places.practical: Book a timed slot online and treat the 5 dollar booking charge as part of the price when you compare against other observatories. Avoid the hour either side of sunset unless you are prepared to queue. Weather decides this attraction more than any other in the city, so pick a clear day and use a flexible ticket if your dates allow.
places.tickets: Main deck 86th floor tickets start at 44 dollars, with a 5 dollar booking charge added to each transaction. Upgraded and flexible ticket types cost more and allow rescheduling.
places.getting_there: 34th Street Herald Square on the B, D, F, M, N, Q, R and W lines is two blocks away. 34th Street Penn Station on the 1, 2, 3, A, C and E lines is a short walk west.
places.location_context: Midtown Manhattan on Fifth Avenue at 34th Street, in a dense commercial district next to Herald Square and Macy's. It is functional rather than charming at street level, and Bryant Park and Koreatown are both a short walk for somewhere better to eat.
places.time_needed: Around ninety minutes including security, the lift and time on the deck. Longer if you add the 102nd floor or arrive near sunset.
places.accessibility: Both observation decks are reached by lift and the building publishes accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: Still the best paid high view in New York, mostly because it is open-air and centrally placed. Book off-peak, stay on the 86th floor, and remember the 5 dollar booking charge when you are comparing it against the alternatives.

places.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
places.headline: Oysters Under the Vaulted Tiles, Weekdays Until Half Nine
places.body:
The Grand Central Oyster Bar is at 89 East 42nd Street on the lower level of Grand Central Terminal, and opens Monday to Friday from 11:30am to 9:30pm.

It has been there since the terminal opened in 1913, under Rafael Guastavino's tiled vaults, which are the reason to sit at the counter rather than in the dining room. The whispering gallery outside the entrance is the same tilework and is free.

The menu is enormous and inconsistent. Order oysters, the pan roast, and very little else, and it is one of the best lunches in Manhattan.
places.what_great: Guastavino's tiled vaults, which are worth the visit alone. A raw bar with dozens of varieties listed by origin. The pan roast, made in a steam kettle at the counter in front of you.
places.what_ruined: The menu runs to pages and much of it is ordinary. Prices have crept well above what the room implies. It is inside a commuter terminal, so the noise and the churn at 6pm are considerable.
places.rating_rationale: Four for the room and the raw bar. Five for safety inside Grand Central. Three for value: oysters and the pan roast justify it, and a great deal of the rest of the menu does not.
places.meta_description: The Grand Central Oyster Bar sits on the lower level of Grand Central Terminal, open weekdays 11:30am to 9:30pm. Order oysters and the pan roast.

places.what_it_is: A seafood restaurant and raw bar on the lower level of Grand Central Terminal, open since 1913, under vaulted Guastavino tilework.
places.why_go: For the room, which is one of the great interiors in New York, and for a raw bar that lists its oysters by bed rather than by colour.
places.the_good: The tiled vaults, a serious oyster list, the pan roast made at the counter, and a lunch that fits neatly around a train.
places.the_downsides: An unwieldy menu with plenty of filler. Prices above what the setting suggests. Loud and hectic at commuter hours.
places.best_for: Anyone passing through Grand Central, and anyone who wants oysters without a downtown scene attached.
places.skip_if: You want a quiet dinner. This is a terminal restaurant and behaves like one.
places.practical: Sit at the counter, not in the dining room, because the counter is where the vaults and the kettles are. Order oysters and a pan roast and stop there. Go at 2pm to avoid both rushes.
places.tickets: A la carte, with market prices on the raw bar. No reservations at the counter; the dining room takes them.
places.getting_there: Inside Grand Central Terminal, lower level. Subway 4, 5, 6, 7 and S to Grand Central-42nd Street.
places.location_context: The lower dining concourse of Grand Central Terminal in Midtown East, directly beneath the main concourse and beside the whispering gallery.
places.time_needed: An hour.
places.verdict: Sit at the counter, order oysters and the pan roast, and ignore the rest of the menu. The room is worth it on its own.

places.name: Hotel Chelsea
places.headline: Two Hundred Square Feet, and More History Than Any Room in New York
places.body:
Rooms at the Hotel Chelsea start small: the Petite Chelsea is a queen bed at 200 sq ft, about 19 sq m. Accessible rooms are larger, with a king bed at approximately 450 sq ft, and are booked by emailing the hotel rather than online. Nightly rates are not published as a fixed figure.

The building on West 23rd Street housed Dylan Thomas, Patti Smith, Leonard Cohen, Janis Joplin and Sid Vicious, and spent a decade closed for a restoration that was widely expected to sand all of that away. It did not: the staircase, the ironwork and a good deal of the art survived.

There is a lobby bar, El Quijote next door, and a Japanese restaurant in the building, which between them mean you need not leave in the evening.
places.what_great: A building with a genuine claim on twentieth-century culture, restored rather than gutted. The staircase and the lobby art. El Quijote, which reopened with the hotel and is worth a table on its own.
places.what_ruined: Standard rooms are genuinely small at 200 sq ft. The history draws people who want to look rather than stay, so the lobby is busy. No published rates, and accessible rooms cannot be booked online at all.
places.rating_rationale: Four for a restoration that kept what mattered. Five for safety in Chelsea. Three for value: Manhattan pricing for a small room, bought largely for the address and the history.
places.meta_description: The Hotel Chelsea's Petite rooms are 200 sq ft; accessible rooms are about 450 sq ft and booked by email. Rates are not published.

places.what_it_is: A landmark hotel on West 23rd Street in Chelsea, Manhattan, reopened after a long restoration, with rooms from 200 sq ft, a lobby bar, El Quijote and a Japanese restaurant in the building.
places.why_go: For the building. Very few hotels anywhere have this much cultural history still legible in the fabric, and the restoration kept the staircase, the ironwork and the art rather than replacing them.
places.the_good: A genuinely historic building handled with care, the staircase and lobby art, El Quijote next door, and a Chelsea address within walking distance of the High Line and the Village.
places.the_downsides: Small standard rooms. A lobby that functions partly as a tourist attraction. No published rates, and accessible rooms require emailing to book.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in twentieth-century music, writing or art, and anyone who would rather stay somewhere specific than somewhere large.
places.skip_if: You need space, or you want a quiet anonymous hotel. Neither describes this building.
places.practical: Book above the Petite category if 200 sq ft sounds tight, because it is. Accessible rooms have to be arranged by email, so allow time. Eat at El Quijote at least once.

places.location_context: West 23rd Street in Chelsea, walking distance to the High Line, Chelsea Market, the gallery district and the West Village.
places.time_needed: Two to three nights.
places.verdict: Stay for the building, and book a category above Petite. The restoration kept what mattered, which almost no one expected.

places.name: Katz's Delicatessen
places.headline: Open Eight Until Eleven, and Straight Through the Weekend
places.body:
Katz's Delicatessen opens Monday to Thursday from 8:00 am to 11:00 pm, and runs continuously from 8:00 am Friday to 11:00 pm Sunday. It has been on the corner of Houston and Ludlow since 1888.

The system is the thing people get wrong. You are handed a ticket at the door, you take it to a carver at the counter, you tip the carver, and you keep the ticket until you leave. Losing it is expensive. The tables at the back have waiter service and a longer wait.

Order the pastrami on rye. Everything else on that enormous menu exists, and none of it is why anyone has been queueing here for a hundred and thirty-seven years.
places.what_great: Pastrami cured on the premises for weeks and cut by hand in front of you. Open continuously from Friday morning to Sunday night, which almost nothing else does. A room that has not been redesigned into something else.
places.what_ruined: Expensive for a sandwich, and it has become a destination as much as a deli. The ticket system baffles first-timers and losing the ticket carries a penalty. Queues run down the block at weekend lunchtimes.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the pastrami, which genuinely is the best version of the thing. Four for safety on a busy Lower East Side corner. Three for value: the sandwich costs what a full meal costs elsewhere, and it does feed two.
places.meta_description: Katz's Delicatessen in New York opens 8am to 11pm Monday to Thursday and runs continuously through the weekend. Take a ticket, tip the carver.

places.what_it_is: A Jewish delicatessen on the corner of East Houston and Ludlow on the Lower East Side, open since 1888, curing and hand-carving its own pastrami.
places.why_go: For the pastrami on rye, which is the reference version, and for a room that has resisted every temptation to become something more fashionable.
places.the_good: Pastrami cured for weeks in house and carved by hand, weekend opening around the clock, and the counter system once you understand it.
places.the_downsides: Very expensive for a sandwich. Long queues. A confusing ticket system with a penalty for losing it. Heavily touristed.
places.best_for: Any first visit to New York, and anyone who wants to understand what the fuss about pastrami actually is.
places.skip_if: You are vegetarian, or you object on principle to queueing for food.
places.practical: Take a ticket at the door and do not lose it. Go to the counter rather than the table service, tip the carver a couple of dollars and you will get a taste while you wait. Share one sandwich between two.
places.tickets: A la carte. No reservations. Counter service by ticket, table service at the back.
places.getting_there: Subway F to Second Avenue, then two minutes on foot. It is on the corner of East Houston Street and Ludlow Street.
places.location_context: The Lower East Side at the Houston Street boundary, an area of bars and boutiques now, with this and a handful of other survivors from when it was not.
places.time_needed: An hour, longer if the queue is out the door.
places.verdict: Take a ticket, go to the counter, tip the carver, order pastrami on rye and share it. Ignore the rest of the menu entirely.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden
places.headline: Thirty-Five Dollars, Free to New Yorkers on Wednesdays, and Worth the Train
places.body:
The New York Botanical Garden charges a weekday adult all-garden pass of 35 dollars, with 31 for seniors and students and 15 for children. Children under 2 are no charge. On Wednesdays, grounds admission is free to New York City residents all day.

The garden is 250 acres in the Bronx, which is a scale New Yorkers rarely encounter. Inside it is the Enid A. Haupt Conservatory, a Victorian-style glasshouse from 1902, and a fifty-acre stand of old-growth forest that has never been logged, the last remnant of the woodland that covered the whole city.

That forest is the argument for coming. Everything else here exists elsewhere; a never-logged New York forest does not.
places.what_great: Two hundred and fifty acres and a fifty-acre old-growth forest, which is unlike anything else reachable on a Metro-North ticket. The 1902 conservatory is a serious piece of Victorian glasshouse architecture. Free grounds admission for NYC residents on Wednesdays, and children under 2 are no charge.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-five dollars for a weekday adult is steep next to Central Park, which is free. It is in the Bronx, so it costs a train ride and most of a day. The all-garden pass and grounds-only admission are different products and the difference is easy to miss when booking.
places.rating_rationale: Four because 250 acres with a Victorian glasshouse and old-growth forest is a genuinely different New York day. Value is three: 35 dollars on a weekday is a lot unless you are a city resident going on a Wednesday, when the grounds are free.
places.meta_description: The New York Botanical Garden costs 35 dollars weekday adult, and grounds admission is free to NYC residents on Wednesdays.
