places.what_it_is: The state gallery of Venetian art, in the former Scuola della Carita and adjoining convent at the southern foot of the Accademia bridge, holding Venetian painting from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century.
places.why_go: Because Venetian painting is the thing Venice actually produced, and this is where it is. Giorgione's Tempest, Bellini, Titian, Tintoretto, Veronese's Feast in the House of Levi and Leonardo's Vitruvian Man are all here.
places.the_good: A first-rank collection at 20 euros, with 2 euros for EU citizens aged 18 to 25 and free entry for under 18s. It is quiet in a city where nothing else is. Buying online lets you skip the ticket office queue.
places.the_downsides: Labelling is thin and assumes prior knowledge. Twenty euros stings in a city that charges for everything. Online sales run through a single authorised operator, so anything else you find online is not the official channel.
places.best_for: Anyone with an interest in Renaissance painting, EU citizens aged 18 to 25 who effectively get it for 2 euros, and any visitor who has had enough of the San Marco crush.
places.skip_if: You have one day in Venice and have never been, in which case the city itself and the Basilica come first. Skip it also if you want context and explanation rather than paintings, since the labelling will not provide it.
places.practical: Buy online through the authorised operator to skip the ticket office. Go in the morning while the crowd is at San Marco. If you are an EU citizen aged 18 to 25, bring ID, because the 2 euro rate is worth having the document for.
places.tickets: Full price is 20,00 euros. Young persons who are EU citizens aged 18 to 25 pay 2,00 euros, and under 18s enter free. There are free admission days requiring no booking, and online sales run through a single authorised ticketing operator.
places.getting_there: Vaporetto line 1 or 2 to Accademia, which stops at the foot of the bridge outside. It is about a twenty-minute walk from Piazza San Marco across the Accademia bridge.
places.location_context: Dorsoduro, on the south side of the Grand Canal at the Accademia bridge, in the quieter university quarter. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection and the Punta della Dogana are both a short walk east along the same bank.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the full collection at a reasonable pace. Ninety minutes if you go straight for the sixteenth century.
places.verdict: The best-value serious museum in Venice, and the calmest. Go in the morning, buy online, and if you are a young EU citizen the 2 euro rate makes this close to the easiest recommendation on the site.
places.accessibility: Barrier-free entry is on the right side of the museum, on Calle della Carita, with lifts to the first floor and lifting platforms beyond. The route is not complete: between rooms XXII and XXIV on the first floor there are no lifting platforms, which interrupts the accessible route. Worth checking on arrival which sections are reachable that day.

places.name: Palazzo Ducale
places.headline: Thirty-Five Euros at the Door, Thirty If You Book Online
places.body:
Palazzo Ducale charges 35.00 euros for a standard ticket and 15.00 euros reduced, dropping to 30.00 euros standard if bought online in advance. It opens 09:00 to 19:00 from 1 April to 31 October, with last admission at 18:00, and 09:00 to 18:00 in winter.

The ticket is not only for the palace. It covers the Musei di Piazza San Marco, so the Correr Museum and the archaeological museum come with it, which changes the value calculation considerably if you use them.

Inside, the sequence that matters is the Doge's apartments, the enormous Sala del Maggior Consiglio with Tintoretto's Paradise, and then the Bridge of Sighs into the prisons, walked in the direction the condemned walked. It is the best-preserved seat of a vanished republic in Europe.
places.what_great: Five euros saved by booking online, and one ticket covering three museums on the square. Tintoretto's Paradise is the largest old master painting in the world and the room does it justice. The prison route is genuinely atmospheric.
places.what_ruined: Thirty-five euros at the door is among the highest museum prices in Italy, and Piazza San Marco in July is a scrum from the moment it opens. The one-way route means you cannot go back for a second look, and the Bridge of Sighs is a two-second shuffle in a queue.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the single most important building in Venice. Four for safety, purely for pickpocketing risk in the queues on the piazza. Four for value: expensive, but it covers three museums and the online price is meaningfully lower.
places.meta_description: Palazzo Ducale in Venice costs 35 euros standard, 30 online, and covers the Musei di Piazza San Marco. Open 09:00 to 19:00 in summer.

places.what_it_is: The seat of the Doge and the government of the Venetian Republic for a thousand years, on Piazza San Marco, now a museum covering the state rooms, the armoury, the Bridge of Sighs and the prisons.
places.why_go: It is the building the republic ran from, and it survives more or less intact. Tintoretto's Paradise and the Sala del Maggior Consiglio explain Venetian power more directly than any book about it.
places.the_good: Genuinely magnificent state rooms, the largest old master painting in the world, the prisons and the Bridge of Sighs, and a ticket that also covers the Correr and the archaeological museum.
places.the_downsides: Very expensive at the door. Extremely crowded in summer. A fixed one-way route with no backtracking. The Bridge of Sighs is a brief shuffle rather than a moment.
places.best_for: Every first-time visitor to Venice, and anyone interested in how a maritime republic actually governed itself.
places.skip_if: You are in Venice for a day and would rather spend it in the quieter sestieri. In that case the Accademia is a calmer use of the money.
places.practical: Book online and save five euros, then arrive at opening. Use the Correr on the same ticket rather than letting it go to waste. Last admission is an hour before closing, which is not enough time to do the route properly.
places.tickets: Standard 35.00 euros, reduced 15.00 euros, and 30.00 euros standard when purchased online in advance. The ticket includes the Musei di Piazza San Marco. Venetian residents and various categories enter free.
places.getting_there: Vaporetto line 1 or 2 to San Marco or San Zaccaria, then a two-minute walk. From the railway station it is a forty-minute walk or a twenty-five-minute vaporetto ride.
places.location_context: The eastern corner of Piazza San Marco, beside the basilica and facing the lagoon, which is the single most concentrated tourist site in Italy.
places.time_needed: Two to three hours for the full route including the prisons.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve most of the state rooms, but the prisons and Bridge of Sighs involve stairs and narrow passages that are not step-free.
places.verdict: Book online, save the five euros, arrive at nine, and use the Correr on the same ticket. Expensive, unavoidable, and worth it.

places.name: Figlmuller
places.headline: The Schnitzel Bigger Than the Plate, at Two Addresses Five Minutes Apart
places.body:
Figlmuller has two branches in the old town. Backerstrasse 6 is open daily 11:30am to 11:30pm with the kitchen running to 10pm, and Wollzeile 5 is open daily 11am to 10:30pm.

The schnitzel is the point: pounded until it overhangs the plate on every side, fried in a succession of pans, and served with potato salad rather than anything hot. It is pork rather than veal, which purists complain about and which is stated plainly on the menu.

The Wollzeile branch, down a covered passage, is the original and the more crowded. Backerstrasse is larger, later, and easier to get into, and the schnitzel is identical.
places.what_great: A genuinely enormous, genuinely well-made schnitzel. Two branches five minutes apart, which doubles your chance of a table. Open daily, which in Vienna is not a given.
places.what_ruined: Queues at Wollzeile that people join without realising the other branch exists. It is pork, not veal, so anyone expecting a Wiener Schnitzel in the strict sense should order accordingly. Service is efficient in the way of a place that turns tables fast.
places.rating_rationale: Four for doing one thing extremely well. Five for safety in the old town. Four for value: not cheap, but the portion genuinely feeds two people who are not especially hungry.

places.what_it_is: A Viennese schnitzel house with two branches in the first district, serving a pounded, plate-overhanging pork schnitzel with potato salad since 1905.
places.why_go: For the schnitzel, which is the version of the dish Vienna is famous for and is done here at a scale that is genuinely funny the first time it arrives.
places.the_good: An excellent, enormous schnitzel. Two branches within five minutes of each other. Daily opening, late at Backerstrasse. Potato salad that is better than it needs to be.
places.the_downsides: Queues at the original branch. Pork rather than veal. Brisk table-turning. The dining rooms are tight.
places.best_for: Any first visit to Vienna, and anyone happy to share, because one schnitzel is close to two portions.
places.skip_if: You specifically want veal Wiener Schnitzel, in which case Figlmuller sells that too but it is not what the queue is for.
places.practical: Book, or go to Backerstrasse rather than Wollzeile, which is larger and open later for the same food. Order one schnitzel between two if you also want a starter.
places.tickets: A la carte, no set menu. Reservations taken online for both branches and strongly advised in the evening.
places.getting_there: U1 or U3 to Stephansplatz, then two to five minutes on foot. Wollzeile is reached through a covered passage off the street.
places.location_context: The first district, immediately east of St Stephen's cathedral, in the dense grid of lanes between Stephansplatz and the Ringstrasse.
places.time_needed: An hour and a half.
places.verdict: Go to the Backerstrasse branch, not the queue at Wollzeile, and share one schnitzel unless you are very hungry.

places.name: Hofburg Imperial Palace
places.headline: Twenty Euros for the Sisi Myth, Told Better Than You Expect
places.body:
The Hofburg charges 20,00 euros for adults and 12,00 euros for children from age 6, on fixed admission times, with the standard route running about 60 minutes.

What the ticket buys is three things in sequence: the Imperial Apartments, the Sisi Museum and the Silver Collection. The Sisi Museum is the reason most people come and it is better than its subject matter suggests, because it spends much of its length dismantling the sentimental version of Empress Elisabeth that Austrian tourism otherwise sells hard.

Fixed admission times matter here. This is not a come-when-you-like palace, and turning up without a slot in high season is how people end up eating lunch instead.
places.what_great: The Sisi Museum treats its subject critically rather than as merchandise, which is rare for a national icon. One ticket covers three collections in a single route. Children from six pay 12 euros, and the whole thing takes about an hour, so it fits into a day rather than consuming one.
places.what_ruined: Fixed admission times mean the visit has to be planned around. The route is one-way and busy through the middle of the day. The gift-shop version of Sisi outside the museum flatly contradicts the honest account inside it, which is a strange note to leave on.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the Sisi Museum is unusually honest about the difference between the woman and the legend built on her. Value is four: 20 euros covers three linked attractions and children from six pay 12.

places.what_it_is: The winter residence of the Habsburgs in central Vienna, now a visitor route through the Imperial Apartments, the Sisi Museum devoted to Empress Elisabeth, and the Silver Collection of the imperial household.
places.why_go: For the Sisi Museum, which is a genuinely thoughtful account of a woman who has been turned into a tourism product, and for state rooms that show how the Habsburgs actually lived rather than how they were painted.
places.the_good: Three collections on one ticket, a route that takes about an hour, and a museum that argues with its own legend instead of selling it. Children from age 6 pay 12,00 euros, which makes it viable for families in an expensive city.
places.the_downsides: Fixed admission times remove any flexibility from the day. The corridors are narrow and the middle of the day is congested. Photography is restricted in much of the route.
places.best_for: First-time visitors to Vienna, anyone interested in the Habsburgs, and families given the child rate. It also works well as a shorter indoor stop between larger museums.
places.skip_if: You are choosing between this and Schonbrunn on a short trip. Schonbrunn has the gardens and the scale; the Hofburg has the better museum. Pick one rather than doing both badly.
places.practical: Book a fixed admission time rather than hoping to walk up. Sixty minutes is the honest allowance for the standard route. Go early or late, since the middle of the day is when tour groups move through.
places.tickets: Adults pay 20,00 euros and children from age 6 pay 12,00 euros. Admission times are fixed, and the standard route runs about 60 minutes.
places.getting_there: U3 to Herrengasse or U1 and U3 to Stephansplatz, both a short walk. Trams 1, 2, D and 71 stop on the Ring at Burgring.
places.location_context: Dead centre of Vienna inside the Ring, between the Michaelerplatz and the Heldenplatz, with the Spanish Riding School in the same complex and the Kunsthistorisches Museum across the Ringstrasse.
places.time_needed: About 60 minutes for the standard route, which is what the fixed admission times are built around. Ninety minutes if you read everything in the Sisi Museum.
places.verdict: Better than it sounds, mostly because the Sisi Museum refuses to play along with the myth it exists to explain. Book a time slot, allow an hour, and treat the gift shop as a separate and less honest experience.
places.accessibility: All exhibition areas are reachable by ramp, mobile wheelchair rails and lift, and wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge against a deposit of identification. Accessible parking is on Heldenplatz.

places.name: Hotel Sacher Vienna
places.headline: Behind the Opera, With the Cafe Open Until Eleven
places.body:
Cafe Sacher Vienna is open Monday to Sunday from 7 am to 11 pm, and the hotel's Rote Bar restaurant runs Monday to Sunday from 12 pm to 12 am. Room rates are not published as a fixed list and move with the season.

The hotel sits directly behind the State Opera, which is the reason to stay here rather than anywhere else at the price: you can leave a performance and be in your room in ninety seconds. The Sachertorte is made on the premises and sold in boxes at the door, which produces a permanent queue that has nothing to do with the hotel.

Rooms are heavily traditional, red and gilt and oil paintings, and the hotel does not apologise for it. Anyone hoping for Scandinavian restraint should book elsewhere.
places.what_great: Ninety seconds from the State Opera. A cafe open from 7 am to 11 pm, which covers both a pre-opera coffee and a post-opera slice. Service in the old European style, done properly.
places.what_ruined: The cake queue outside is constant and can make arriving with luggage awkward. The decoration is maximalist and dark. Among the most expensive hotels in Vienna and, as with all of them, no fixed rate is published.
places.rating_rationale: Five for the hotel and the position behind the opera. Five for safety in the first district. Three for value: you are paying for the address and the name, both of which are real, neither of which is cheap.
places.meta_description: Hotel Sacher Vienna sits behind the State Opera, with Cafe Sacher open daily 7 am to 11 pm and the Rote Bar from noon to midnight.

places.what_it_is: A grand hotel on Philharmoniker Strasse directly behind the Vienna State Opera, open since 1876, with its own cafe, the Rote Bar restaurant and the original Sachertorte made on site.
places.why_go: For the opera. Being ninety seconds from the door of the Staatsoper changes what an evening performance costs you in time and logistics, and nothing else at this level is as close.
places.the_good: The position behind the opera, a cafe open sixteen hours a day, the Rote Bar, and a level of traditional service that has largely disappeared elsewhere.
places.the_downsides: A permanent cake queue at the door. Dense traditional decoration that reads as heavy to modern eyes. Top-of-market pricing with no published rate card.
places.best_for: Anyone going to the opera, and anyone who wants Vienna's imperial register rather than its modern one.
places.skip_if: You want contemporary design or a quiet arrival. The seventh district has better-value hotels with more space.
places.practical: Use the Philharmoniker Strasse entrance rather than pushing through the cake queue. If you are going to the opera, book dinner in the Rote Bar before rather than after, because the kitchen is busiest at the interval.
places.tickets: Room rates are not published as a fixed list and vary with season and availability. Cafe Sacher and the Rote Bar are open to non-residents and take reservations.
places.getting_there: U1, U2 or U4 to Karlsplatz, then three minutes on foot, or trams 1, 2, 71 and D to Oper. From the airport, the City Airport Train to Wien Mitte then one metro stop.
places.location_context: Philharmoniker Strasse in the first district, wedged between the State Opera and the Albertina, two minutes from the Hofburg and five from Stephansplatz.
places.time_needed: Two nights, or one if you are here for a single performance.
places.verdict: Stay here if you are going to the opera and the price is survivable. The address is doing most of the work, and the address is genuinely worth it.

places.name: Kunst Haus Wien
places.headline: Sixteen Euros for the Building Hundertwasser Built to Argue With Straight Lines
places.body:
Kunst Haus Wien charges 16,00 euros for admission, with 13,00 for reduced tickets and for seniors 65 and over. Accompanying persons of people with disabilities receive free admission.

The museum is Hundertwasser's own, built in a converted furniture factory, and it is the clearest place to understand what he was actually arguing for: uneven floors on purpose, no straight lines where he could avoid them, trees growing out of the windows.

It is a short visit and an unusually physical one. You notice the building through your feet before you notice any of the paintings, which is precisely the point he was making.
places.what_great: The building is the argument and you experience it directly rather than reading about it. Sixteen euros is cheap by Vienna museum standards and 13 covers both reduced tickets and over-65s. Accompanying persons of visitors with disabilities go free.
places.what_ruined: It is small, and if Hundertwasser does not interest you there is not much else. The deliberately uneven floors are genuinely awkward for anyone unsteady on their feet. It sits away from the central museum cluster, so it costs a journey.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building is a genuine one-off and the museum is small enough to enjoy. Value is four: 16 euros is modest for Vienna and the concessions are wide.
places.meta_description: Kunst Haus Wien costs 16 euros, 13 reduced and for over-65s. The Hundertwasser museum, and why the floor is the exhibit.

places.what_it_is: A museum in Landstrasse designed by Friedensreich Hundertwasser inside a converted Thonet furniture factory, holding the permanent collection of his work alongside changing photography and ecology exhibitions.
places.why_go: Because the building makes his case better than his paintings do. Uneven floors, irregular windows and planted trees are not decoration here, they are the thesis, and you walk through it.
places.the_good: A genuine architectural one-off you can walk around in, at 16,00 euros, which is modest for Vienna. Wide concessions at 13,00 for reduced and over-65s, and free entry for companions of disabled visitors. Small enough to see properly in an hour.
places.the_downsides: Narrow appeal outside Hundertwasser and ecological design. The intentionally uneven floors are a real accessibility obstacle rather than a quirk. It is a tram ride from the centre, which is a lot for a one-hour museum unless you pair it with something.
places.best_for: Anyone interested in twentieth-century architecture or environmental design, visitors who have already done the big Ring museums, and travellers who prefer small museums to exhausting ones.
places.skip_if: You have two days in Vienna and have not yet seen the Belvedere or the Kunsthistorisches. Those come first. Skip it also if uneven ground is a problem for you, because that is unavoidable here.
places.practical: Pair it with the Hundertwasserhaus a few streets away, which is a residential building you can only see from outside and costs nothing. An hour covers the museum. Wear shoes you are steady in.
places.tickets: Admission is 16,00 euros, with 13,00 euros for reduced tickets and for seniors 65 and over. Accompanying persons of people with disabilities receive free admission.
places.getting_there: Tram 1 to Radetzkyplatz, or U3 to Rochusgasse and a short walk. It is roughly twenty minutes on foot from Stephansplatz.
places.location_context: Landstrasse, the third district, east of the centre near the Danube canal, in a residential quarter that also contains the Hundertwasserhaus. Quiet, ordinary Vienna rather than the imperial version.
places.time_needed: About an hour for the museum, or ninety minutes with a temporary exhibition. Add twenty minutes to walk to the Hundertwasserhaus.
places.accessibility: Accompanying persons of people with disabilities receive free admission, but the floors are deliberately uneven throughout, which is a genuine obstacle for anyone with limited mobility.
places.verdict: A small, cheap, genuinely unusual museum that is worth the tram ride if the big Ring institutions have worn you out. Go for the building, not the paintings, and check the uneven floors will suit you.

places.name: Upper Belvedere
places.headline: Twenty-Three Euros to Stand in Front of The Kiss, and Under-19s Go Free
places.body:
The Upper Belvedere charges 23,00 euros for an admission ticket, 19,00 euros for seniors over 65 and for students under 26, and nothing at all for children and young people under 19.

What almost everybody comes for is Klimt's The Kiss, which hangs here along with the largest collection of his work anywhere. That concentration is both the attraction and the problem: one room absorbs the crowd while a baroque palace full of Austrian art from the medieval period onward sits comparatively quiet around it.

The building is a Baroque summer palace with formal gardens running down to the Lower Belvedere, and the gardens are free to walk. On a good day that walk is a genuine part of the visit rather than a way of getting between two ticket desks.
places.what_great: The Klimt holding is the best anywhere and The Kiss is genuinely worth the trip. Under-19s get in free and the concession rate covers students up to 26. The gardens between Upper and Lower Belvedere are free and are one of the most pleasant walks in central Vienna.
places.what_ruined: The room holding The Kiss is congested for most of the day and people queue to photograph it rather than look at it. The 23 euro ticket covers the Upper Belvedere only, so a full visit to both palaces costs more. The rest of the collection is unfairly overlooked as a result of the Klimt concentration.
places.rating_rationale: Four because the building and the collection are both excellent, held back only by how hard the crowd concentrates on one painting. Value is four: 23 euros is fair, and free entry for everyone under 19 is a real family saving.
places.meta_description: The Upper Belvedere costs 23 euros, 19 for over-65s and students under 26, and is free for under-19s. Where Klimt hangs and when to go.

places.what_it_is: A Baroque palace on the upper terrace of the Belvedere complex, built for Prince Eugene of Savoy and now a museum of Austrian art holding the world's largest collection of Gustav Klimt paintings, including The Kiss.
places.why_go: For Klimt, and specifically for The Kiss, which is one of the few paintings that genuinely rewards the trip. The Baroque palace interior and the view down the gardens toward the city are the second reason.
places.the_good: The Klimt rooms are unmatched, the building is a first-rank Baroque palace in its own right, and the gardens outside cost nothing. Free entry for everyone under 19 and a 19 euro rate for students under 26 and over-65s make it accessible for families and young travellers.
places.the_downsides: The Kiss draws a persistent crowd and the room around it is the least comfortable part of the museum. The 23 euro ticket is for the Upper Belvedere alone, so seeing the Lower Belvedere as well means paying again. Much of the rest of the collection goes unlooked-at.
places.best_for: Anyone who wants to see Klimt properly, visitors interested in Baroque architecture, and families given the free under-19 entry.
places.skip_if: You have limited time in Vienna and a broader interest in art history, in which case the Kunsthistorisches Museum covers far more ground. Skip it if crowds around a single famous painting are the thing you most dislike about museums.
places.practical: Go at opening or in the last two hours; the Klimt room is markedly calmer at both ends of the day. Walk the gardens down to the Lower Belvedere afterwards, which is free. Buy online to avoid the ticket queue, which is separate from the entry queue.
places.tickets: An admission ticket to the Upper Belvedere is 23,00 euros. Seniors over 65 and students under 26 pay 19,00 euros. Children and young people under 19 pay nothing. Holders of a valid Vienna City Card receive a discount.
places.getting_there: Tram D to Schloss Belvedere for the upper entrance, or tram 18 and O to Quartier Belvedere. Wien Hauptbahnhof is roughly a ten-minute walk.
places.location_context: Landstrasse, the third district, on rising ground south-east of the Ringstrasse, with the formal gardens running downhill to the Lower Belvedere and the city skyline beyond. It is a quiet, embassy-heavy quarter well away from the Stephansplatz crowds.
places.time_needed: Ninety minutes to two hours for the Upper Belvedere. Add another hour if you walk the gardens and continue to the Lower Belvedere.
places.accessibility: The palace is served by lifts and the Belvedere publishes accessibility information for visitors with reduced mobility.
places.verdict: Worth the 23 euros for the Klimt rooms alone, and better value than it looks once you count the free gardens. Go early, and if you are under 19, or travelling with anyone who is, the arithmetic is even easier.

places.name: Copernicus Science Centre
places.headline: Forty-Eight Zloty on a Weekday, Fifty at the Weekend
places.body:
The Copernicus Science Centre charges 48 zloty for a full-price exhibition ticket on weekdays and 50 zloty at weekends and on holidays, with reduced tickets at 34 and 36 zloty. Children under 2 enter free.

It is the best science centre in central Europe and it is not close. Around 450 hands-on exhibits across several floors, a high-voltage theatre with a genuine Tesla coil, a robotics gallery, and a planetarium that is ticketed separately.

The building sits on the Vistula embankment with a roof garden looking over the river, which makes it a rare Warsaw attraction that works as a half day out rather than a single stop.
places.what_great: Enormous, genuinely hands-on, and priced within reach at 48 zloty. The high-voltage theatre is a real crowd-stopper. The riverside setting and roof garden are a bonus most science centres cannot offer.
places.what_ruined: It is aimed squarely at children and is loud and busy accordingly, particularly at weekends and during school holidays. Tickets are timed and sell out. The planetarium costs extra on top.
places.rating_rationale: Four because adults without children will find it aimed elsewhere. Five for safety. Five for value: 48 zloty for 450 exhibits and half a day is excellent.

places.what_it_is: A large hands-on science centre on the Vistula embankment in central Warsaw, with several themed galleries, a high-voltage theatre, a robotics section and a separately ticketed planetarium.
places.why_go: It is the strongest family attraction in Poland and among the best science centres in Europe, and the price is a fraction of what the equivalent costs in western capitals.
places.the_good: Around 450 exhibits that genuinely work, a memorable high-voltage show, long opening hours, a riverside roof garden, and honest weekday and weekend pricing.
places.the_downsides: Noisy and crowded with school groups. Timed tickets sell out at weekends. The planetarium is an additional charge. Adults visiting alone are not the target audience.
places.best_for: Families with children between about six and fifteen, and anyone travelling with teenagers who need a day that is not another church.
places.skip_if: You are in Warsaw for the history. The Rising Museum and the old town will serve you better.
places.practical: Book a weekday slot online if you can, which is both cheaper and quieter. Allow three hours minimum. Decide about the planetarium before you arrive, because it is a separate ticket and separate timing.
places.tickets: Exhibition full price 48 zloty on weekdays and 50 zloty at weekends and holidays; reduced 34 and 36 zloty. Reduced rates cover pupils, students and PhD candidates under 26, seniors over 60 and people with a disability. Children under 2 enter free.
places.getting_there: Metro line 2 to Centrum Nauki Kopernik, which surfaces directly outside, or a twenty-minute walk from the old town along the river.
places.location_context: The Powisle riverside, below the escarpment that carries the old town, next to the university library roof garden and a short walk from the Vistula boulevards.
places.time_needed: Three to four hours, longer with children who refuse to leave.
places.accessibility: Step-free throughout with lifts to all galleries, and free entry for an assistant accompanying a person with a disability.
places.verdict: The best family day in Warsaw and cheap for what it is. Book a weekday slot, allow three hours, and treat the planetarium as a separate decision.

places.name: Warsaw Rising Museum
places.headline: Thirty-Five Zloty for Sixty-Three Days That Destroyed a City
places.body:
The Warsaw Rising Museum charges 35 PLN for a normal ticket and 30 PLN discounted, with a large family card ticket at 10 PLN per person. It opens Monday and Wednesday to Friday from 8am to 6pm, Saturday and Sunday from 10am to 6pm, and is closed on Tuesdays.

The museum covers the uprising of August and September 1944, when the Polish underground took on the German garrison expecting Soviet support that never came. Sixty-three days later the rising had failed and the city was systematically demolished in reprisal.

The design is deliberately overwhelming: a beating-heart soundtrack through the whole building, a walk-through sewer of the kind the insurgents used to move between districts, and a short film reconstructing the flight over the flattened city. It does not attempt neutrality and does not pretend to.
places.what_great: Thirty-five zloty for one of the most powerful museums in Europe. The reconstructed sewer and the City of Ruins film are unforgettable. Opens at 8am on most weekdays, which no other major museum in Warsaw does.
places.what_ruined: Dark, loud and emotionally heavy, and not remotely suitable for young children. The layout is confusing and easy to walk out of order. Closed on Tuesdays, which is not obvious to visitors used to Monday closures.
places.rating_rationale: Five for a museum that does something no other does. Five for safety in Wola. Five for value: 35 zloty is about seven euros for three hours of the best exhibition design in the region.

places.what_it_is: A museum in a former tram power station in Wola devoted to the Warsaw Rising of 1944, its sixty-three days of fighting, and the destruction of the city that followed.
places.why_go: It explains modern Warsaw. The reason the city is mostly postwar concrete and reconstructed old town is contained entirely in this building, and no account of Poland's twentieth century makes sense without it.
places.the_good: Outstanding exhibition design, the walk-through sewer, the City of Ruins aerial film, early opening hours, and a price that puts it within reach of everyone.
places.the_downsides: Emotionally punishing and unsuitable for young children. The route is not clearly linear. Closed Tuesdays. Busy with school groups in term time.
places.best_for: Anyone visiting Warsaw for the first time, and anyone interested in the Second World War beyond the western front.
places.skip_if: You are travelling with small children, or you want a light morning. This is neither.
places.practical: Arrive at 8am on a weekday when it opens, which is genuinely quiet. Allow three hours. The audio guide hire is 13 PLN and worth it, because the labelling assumes context. Watch the City of Ruins film at the end, not the start.
places.tickets: Normal 35 PLN, discounted 30 PLN, group ticket 35 PLN with a museum guide booked online, large family card holders 10 PLN per person at the box office. Audio guide hire is 13 PLN.
places.getting_there: Tram to Muzeum Powstania Warszawskiego, or a twenty-minute walk west from Rondo Daszynskiego metro station.
places.location_context: Wola, west of the centre, an area that was the site of the worst massacres of the rising and is now largely rebuilt offices and apartments.
places.time_needed: Three hours. Two if you skip the film, which would be a mistake.
places.accessibility: Lifts serve the main levels, though the sewer reconstruction is by its nature not accessible.
places.verdict: The single most important museum in Warsaw and thirty-five zloty well spent. Arrive at eight, take the audio guide, and leave the afternoon free afterwards.

places.name: Kunsthaus Zurich
places.headline: Twenty-Four Francs for the Collection, Thirty-One if There Is a Big Show
places.body:
The Kunsthaus Zurich charges CHF 24 for adults for the collection and small exhibitions, or CHF 17 reduced, and CHF 31 for a major exhibition, CHF 22 reduced. Children and young people under 14 are admitted free.

The collection is the reason to come: the largest group of Munch outside Norway, a strong Giacometti holding, Hodler, and a Chipperfield extension that doubled the gallery space in 2021. Zurich Card holders get free admission to the collection.

The Chipperfield building and the original house face each other across Heimplatz and are linked underground, which means the museum is now large enough to need a plan rather than a wander.
places.what_great: The Munch collection, which is the biggest outside Norway, and the Giacometti rooms. Free for under-14s. The Chipperfield extension is a genuinely good gallery building. Zurich Card includes the collection.
places.what_ruined: Swiss prices: CHF 31 for a major show is among the highest in Europe. The two buildings are linked underground in a way that is easy to get wrong, and the cloakroom charges CHF 4 unless you bought online.
places.rating_rationale: Four for an excellent collection in a strong new building. Five for safety in central Zurich. Three for value, because even by Swiss standards CHF 24 to CHF 31 is a lot, softened only by free entry under 14.
places.meta_description: Kunsthaus Zurich costs CHF 24 for the collection and CHF 31 for a major exhibition, free under 14. The largest Munch collection outside Norway.

places.what_it_is: Zurich's principal art museum on Heimplatz, in two buildings linked underground, holding European art from the medieval period to the present with particular strength in Munch, Hodler and Giacometti.
places.why_go: For the Munch rooms, which are the largest holding outside Norway, and for a Swiss collection that explains Hodler and Giacometti properly rather than in passing.
places.the_good: Outstanding Munch and Giacometti, a well-made Chipperfield extension, free entry for under-14s, and inclusion in the Zurich Card for the collection.
places.the_downsides: Expensive even for Switzerland. The two-building layout is confusing on a first visit. The cloakroom charges unless you bought your ticket online.
places.best_for: Anyone with a serious interest in modern European painting, and holders of the Zurich Card, for whom the collection is free.
places.skip_if: You are in Zurich for a day and the weather is good. The lake and the old town are the better call in that case.
places.practical: Buy online, which makes the cloakroom free. Decide in advance whether you want the major exhibition, because the cheaper ticket does not include it. Start in the Chipperfield building and cross underground.
places.tickets: Collection and small exhibitions CHF 24, reduced CHF 17. Major exhibition CHF 31, reduced CHF 22. Free for members and for children and young people under 14. Zurich Card holders enter the collection free.
places.getting_there: Tram 3, 5, 8 or 9 to Kunsthaus, which stops on Heimplatz outside the door. It is a ten-minute walk uphill from Bellevue.
places.location_context: Heimplatz, on the eastern edge of the old town below the university quarter, a short walk from the Grossmunster and the lake.
places.time_needed: Two hours for the collection, three if a major exhibition is on.
places.accessibility: Both buildings are step-free with lifts, and the underground passage between them is level.
places.verdict: Go for the Munch rooms and buy online so the cloakroom is free. Twenty-four francs is steep but the collection earns it; skip the major exhibition unless it is one you came for.

places.name: Swiss National Museum
places.headline: Thirteen Francs, Which in Zurich Counts as Free
places.body:
The Swiss National Museum charges 13 CHF for adults and 10 CHF for concessions, and admits children up to 16 free. The Simply Zurich exhibition is free to everyone.

Thirteen francs is startling in a city where a coffee costs six. It buys the national historical collection, from prehistory through the Confederation to the present, in a purpose-built 1898 castle-like pile immediately behind the main station.

The 2016 extension by Christ and Gantenbein is the other reason to come: a raw concrete addition that folds into the old building and is one of the better pieces of recent Swiss architecture. The armoury and the historical rooms are the collection highlights.
places.what_great: Thirteen francs in Zurich, free for under-16s, and free entry to the Simply Zurich exhibition. Directly behind the main station, so it works as an arrival or departure stop. The Christ and Gantenbein extension is worth seeing on its own.
places.what_ruined: The permanent displays are dense and text-heavy, and the story of the Confederation assumes more prior knowledge than most visitors have. Closed Mondays. The park behind it is pleasant but small.
places.rating_rationale: Four for a solid national museum that is heavier going than it needs to be. Five for safety. Five for value, because 13 CHF is close to the cheapest cultural hour in Switzerland and under-16s are free.
places.meta_description: The Swiss National Museum in Zurich costs 13 CHF for adults and is free for under-16s. National history in an 1898 pile behind the main station.

places.what_it_is: Switzerland's national history museum, immediately behind Zurich main station, covering the country from prehistory to the present in an 1898 building with a 2016 concrete extension.
places.why_go: It is the cheapest serious museum in one of the most expensive cities in the world, and the only place in Zurich that explains how the Confederation came together rather than assuming you know.
places.the_good: Thirteen francs. Free for under-16s. A free Simply Zurich exhibition. Strong armoury and historical interiors, and an excellent modern extension. Two minutes from the station.
places.the_downsides: Text-heavy displays that assume familiarity with Swiss history. Closed Mondays. Some galleries feel dated next to the new wing.
places.best_for: Anyone with a few hours between trains, families given free entry under 16, and anyone curious about how Switzerland actually works.
places.skip_if: You have one clear day and good weather. Uetliberg and the lake are the better use of it.
places.practical: It is two minutes from the main station, so it is the ideal place to spend a long layover. Start with Simply Zurich, which is free, then decide whether to pay for the rest. Closed Mondays.
places.tickets: Adults 13 CHF, concessions including pensioners, pupils and students 10 CHF, children up to 16 free. The Simply Zurich exhibition is free. An annual pass covering all Swiss National Museum sites is 35 CHF.
places.getting_there: Two minutes on foot from Zurich Hauptbahnhof, out of the north end of the station and across the bridge.
places.location_context: Platzspitz, the wedge of park where the Sihl meets the Limmat directly behind the main station, five minutes from Bahnhofstrasse.
places.time_needed: Two hours, or one for the free Simply Zurich exhibition alone.
places.accessibility: Step-free access with lifts throughout both the historic building and the extension.
places.verdict: The best-value hours in Zurich by a distance. Thirteen francs, free under 16, free for the Simply Zurich exhibition, and two minutes from the platforms.

places.name: Zeughauskeller
places.headline: Open Daily From Half Eleven Until Eleven, Sundays Included
places.body:
The Zeughauskeller is open daily from 11.30 am to 11.00 pm, Sundays included, and serves hot meals all day from 11.30 to 22.00. In a city where a great many kitchens close between services and most things shut on Sunday, that is the single most useful fact about it.

The building is a sixteenth-century arsenal and it still looks like one: a vaulted hall, long shared tables, halberds and armour on the walls, and a cannon. The food is Swiss and German in the substantial sense, and the Kalbsgeschnetzeltes and the metre-long sausages are what people order.

It is two minutes from Paradeplatz, which means it is surrounded by banks and is one of very few places in that part of Zurich where a normal person can eat without booking.
places.what_great: Open every day from 11.30 to 23.00 with hot food throughout, which solves the Zurich Sunday problem outright. A genuine sixteenth-century arsenal hall. Walk-ins are normal.
places.what_ruined: Loud, busy and full of tourists at peak times. Swiss prices apply, so a plate of veal and rosti is not cheap. Shared tables are the norm, which not everyone enjoys.
places.rating_rationale: Four for a genuinely historic hall serving solid Swiss food reliably. Five for safety by Paradeplatz. Four for value: expensive in absolute terms, fair for Zurich, and the portions are serious.

places.what_it_is: A large traditional restaurant in a sixteenth-century arsenal building off Paradeplatz in central Zurich, serving Swiss and German food at long shared tables.
places.why_go: For a substantial Swiss meal at almost any hour, in a genuinely old hall, without a reservation. In central Zurich that combination is close to unique.
places.the_good: Daily opening with hot food from 11.30 to 22.00, an arsenal hall complete with armour and a cannon, big portions, and walk-in seating.
places.the_downsides: Noisy and heavily touristed. Swiss prices. Shared tables. The cooking is reliable rather than refined.
places.best_for: First-time visitors, groups, and anyone stuck in Zurich on a Sunday when much of the city is closed.
places.skip_if: You want a quiet dinner or modern Swiss cooking. Neither is on offer here.
places.practical: Walk in rather than book, and go slightly off peak if you want a table to yourself. The mid-afternoon is the best time to see the hall properly. Order the Kalbsgeschnetzeltes with rosti.
places.tickets: A la carte, no set menu. Reservations possible but not necessary outside peak evenings.
places.getting_there: Tram to Paradeplatz, then two minutes on foot down Bahnhofstrasse and left into In Gassen.
places.location_context: In Gassen, just off Paradeplatz in the banking district, a couple of minutes from Bahnhofstrasse and ten from the Grossmunster.
places.time_needed: An hour and a half.
places.verdict: The most useful restaurant in Zurich: open every day, all afternoon, no booking, in a sixteenth-century arsenal. Go mid-afternoon and order the veal.
